item.title: Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?

Submitted by Nabiya Khan on Fri, 09/04/2026 - 20:06
The country harbours a political culture where exercising the right to demonstrate is safer for some than for others
A CJP supporter waves the national flag a day after the resignation of India’s education minister, in Mumbai on 26 July 2026 (Punit Paranjpe/AFP)
Off

As protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi gained momentum this summer, many Muslims urged their children not to participate. 

Some mosque announcements cautioned Muslim youths to stay away - not over any clash with the movement’s ideals, but amid fears of harassment, false charges, hounding and intimidation.

For many students, attending protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar was a way to show they cared enough about the issues facing the country to show up. But Muslim students in today’s India must always weigh the consequences of their actions. 

Other Muslim student activists have spent years languishing in jail, without trial and with little hope of bail. Some have had their homes demolished. 

In the eyes of the government, Muslim comes first, and student later. Staying home might look like political apathy from the outside, but inside the community, it is a safety valve, underscoring the limits of what Muslims in India can afford to do.

For a generation of young Indians, the CJP has made it easier to imagine themselves as political actors. The movement - which started out as a joke after appalling remarks by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who compared unemployed youths to “cockroaches” - quickly moved from social media to the streets. 

As the protests spread nationwide, they attracted large numbers of young people angry about exam failures, unemployment, and the absence of accountability in a system upon which their futures depend. Thousands marched towards parliament, and on 25 July, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

Political exposure

The warnings to Muslim youths, cautioning them against participation in this countrywide movement, did not stem only from fear. They came from a community with years of experience as to what political exposure can mean. 

Protests over the Citizenship Amendment Act, a law that excludes Muslim immigrants and refugees living in India from obtaining citizenship, are part of this same historical memory. The ensuing crackdown culminated in February 2020, when state-orchestrated communal violence in northeastern Delhi killed 53 people, most of them Muslims. 

The violence was followed by arrests under anti-terrorism legislation, with some of those arrested still in jail years later without trial.

For communities that have repeatedly experienced police targeting, surveillance and violence after political mobilisation, caution is based on experience. Despite such fears, some Muslims still participated in the CJP protests; among them was Mohammad Junaid, who alleges that he was subsequently harassed by police. 

You cannot claim to fight the disease, while telling people living with its symptoms that their suffering is a distraction from the real problem

The CJP movement has made a point of saying that its politics belong to young Indians. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has repeatedly argued that Indian politics has spent too long on Hindu-vs-Muslim issues, and that education and employment should take precedence. 

There is a reasonable political frustration behind this argument. A student whose exam has been cancelled should not have to choose a religion before demanding justice. 

For Muslims, however, communal politics is not a subject that can simply be put aside so that everyone can get back to talking about education and jobs. It follows them into those areas. It affects how they are spoken about, how their neighbourhoods are policed, and how their political actions are read.

The history behind this is longer than Prime Minister Narendra Modi or the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Author Vinayak Damodar Savarkar set out the ideological foundations of Hindutva in his 1923 work Essentials of Hindutva, defining the nation through an idea of Hindu cultural belonging that placed Muslims and Christians outside the same conception of national identity. 

Modi’s years in power have merely brought an old majoritarian politics deeper into the institutions and everyday life of the country. 

Language of incitement

There have been vigilante attacks on Muslims, unlawful demolitions of Muslim homes and businesses, and the expulsion of Bengali-speaking Muslims and Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh. Modi himself made Muslims a central target of his 2024 campaign. 

This is the environment in which a Muslim student decides whether a protest is worth attending.

At the same time, the language of incitement coming from the government has continuously shifted. Modi recently revived the term “dimagi Naxal” to refer to an intellectual insurgency, and the BJP quickly turned the phrase into a coordinated meme campaign on social media, targeting CJP protesters, among others. 

Muslims know this language well. They have been called infiltrators, terrorists and anti-national long before the introduction of “dimagi Naxal”. This does not necessarily mean that every Hindu sees Muslims as a threat, but it does mean that political parties can build an electoral advantage by making Muslims the group against which the majority is asked to measure its own safety and interests. 

For Indian Muslims the end times have arrived
Read More »

In a country where the BJP has won a third consecutive national term by pushing a project based on the systemic extermination of Muslims, these politics cannot be treated as background noise.

That is why blanket statements about “fighting for Indian youth” - while avoiding the word “Muslim”, or refusing to discuss Muslim political prisoners - creates a problem. The CJP can decide not to make Muslims its organising constituency, but it cannot assume that refusing to name Muslims makes communal politics less real.

The success of the CJP thus leaves India with a problem larger than exam leaks. The movement showed that young people can organise, sustain pressure, and make a government act. 

A democracy cannot measure the health of its protest culture only by the number of people who turn up. It has to ask who can turn up without calculating how their surname, neighbourhood or religion might affect them after the protests.

The BJP has made communal politics part of everyday life in India. Muslims have lived with its consequences for years: being called infiltrators and security threats, as their neighbourhoods, homes and activities come under increasing scrutiny. 

These are not side issues. You cannot claim to fight the disease, while telling people living with its symptoms that their suffering is a distraction from the real problem. 

A country can have a constitutional right to protest, while still harbouring a political culture where exercising that right is safer for some than for others. That gap is where democracy is tested. India’s young Muslims know this already. The CJP movement should learn it before it can honestly speak for all.

item.title: Developing nations must work together. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With September 12 marking the UN Day for South-South Cooperation, Bangladesh must recognize the importance of cooperation among developing countries and actively work to strengthen its ties.
Indeed, it would not be a mistake to argue that most meaningful development partnerships increasingly lie within the Global South.
This day reflects a shift in global power, knowledge, and innovation. Developing nations now generate a substantial share of global growth, and their collective experience offers solutions far more relevant to our realities than traditional models originating in the developed North.
Bangladesh has repeatedly benefited from exchanges with fellow developing nations, be they agricultural techniques, disaster‑management expertise, digital‑governance models, renewable‑energy solutions, or public health innovations.
It goes without saying that solutions have greater odds of success when there is an exchange of context‑appropriate tools shaped by countries that have confronted similar constraints and pressures.
It must also be stated that Bangladesh is not merely a recipient, and its achievements in community‑based health systems, microfinance, disaster preparedness, and social‑protection programs have become global references for other nations in the Global South.
South-South cooperation allows Bangladesh to share these strengths while gaining new approaches to emerging challenges such as climate shocks, rapid urbanization, food insecurity, and digital transformation.
Given the importance, it is imperative that we deepen this engagement. Too often, cooperation remains limited to conferences, pilot projects, or symbolic agreements.
Bangladesh needs long‑term partnerships, ones that expand joint research, strengthen climate resilience, and reduce dependence on external models that do not align with our local realities.
The Global South’s collective future depends on how effectively its members learn from one another and build systems rooted in solidarity rather than hierarchy.
This cooperation could be a central pillar of a fairer, more resilient future for all of us.

item.title: Protecting the hand that hurts. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Picture a courtroom in Bangladesh. A woman is sitting on a bench, hiding her bruises, and waiting to testify against her own husband who beats her mercilessly.
When her name is called, she suddenly changes her original story, fervently trying to withdraw the case and convince the magistrate that her injuries were rather the result of an accident.
Outside the courtroom, her mother-in-law is standing, waiting for her to take her to the same house, the same husband, and the same violence.
This is not a rare scenario in Bangladesh’s family courts or police stations; rather, it is a pattern so common here that oftentimes the police or the court shows reluctance to even register cases of domestic violence.
Why do these women, despite years of abuse, try to protect their abusers?
To answer this question, let us travel 53 years into the past.
In 1973, four employees (three women and one man) of Kreditbanken Bank in Stockholm were taken hostage by two robbers for six days.
By the time the police were able to free them, they had grown protective of their captors, refusing to testify against the perpetrators and instead raising money for their legal defense.
Psychiatrists called this condition Stockholm Syndrome; a survival response where the victim develops sympathy, even loyalty toward the abuser who controls their fear.
Similarly, among women who are victims of abuse, a long period of intimate violence and torture produces Stockholm Syndrome in the form of fierce trauma bonding, which leads to an unintentional instinct to protect their abuser from consequences of their own.
In Bangladesh’s household scenario, this trauma bond rarely announces itself as a pathology; rather, it looks like a housewife telling her neighbours that the bruises on her face are from an accidental fall down the stairs, a mother telling her daughter to call the injuries on her body marks of a self-inflicted accident, or a young wife defending her husband’s violence as occasional outbursts of anger.
According to analysts, the main reasons for South Asian women experiencing Stockholm Syndrome are financial dependency, fear of social stigma, patriarchal society, and a conviction that suffering silently is a form of loyalty and a badge of honour for women. A woman's own family often supports this idea of protecting the abusive husband at any cost.
This is akin to the boiling-frog pattern, where researchers illustrate that when abuse towards a woman increases gradually, she can lose the ability or the willingness to protect herself or remove herself from the situation.
Based on the irrational belief that the world cannot offer her a better alternative than what she already has, she thus ends up subconsciously developing instincts to protect her abusive partner.
To make things worse, the Domestic Violence Act (2010) in Bangladesh every so often clashes head-on with the involuntary, deep state of self-preservation in women who have been conditioned to defend their abusers.
As a result, police, often reluctantly, send complaints back for domestic violence matters to be settled “domestically.”
Millions of women enable their partners to continue abusing them throughout their relationships. However, putting the onus of standing up to violence on the victims themselves is easy but, by no means, fair.
Instead, we need to ask the difficult questions here.
Why, after all, do the abused women enable their abusers? And why do they keep protecting these sadist oppressors?
A quick glance at these ill-fated women’s formative years will tell you why.
Since their early days, many women see their mothers silently suffer physical and mental torture, verbal assault, and various other forms of hostility in their own house.
These women keep hearing from their family, neighbours, relatives, and everyone else in society that domestic disputes are normal between married couples, that “purush manush ektu emoni hoy, meye der manay nite hoy” (men will be men and women need to adjust), that a woman’s real house is her husband’s house, and that a good wife should prioritize her family honour and endure her husband’s maltreatment at any cost.
The mass media these women become exposed to during the developmental period further normalizes and even glamorizes violence against women.
Many movies, dramas, and even cartoons typically characterize women as damsels in distress and men as their saviors, romanticizing toxic relationships and portraying physical violence as a sign of passionate love.
Essentially, when a woman is repetitively told that she is a nobody without her husband, the narrative gets fixated in her mind.
Sometimes this narrative can become so noxious that women even end up becoming complicit in their husbands’ crimes. In the brutal Ramisa rape and murder case, for instance, the wife of the offender actively took part in the atrocity.
While this woman’s crimes are unforgivable, have we ever stopped to think that perhaps it was Stockholm Syndrome that made her feel compelled to protect her husband?
What can be done to save these women from themselves? Do we really believe that only enforcing stricter laws against domestic violence, getting more women educated, or helping women become financially independent will solve the issue?
Admittedly, a combined effort from all these fronts will likely improve the situation to a certain extent. However, until and unless our society recalibrates its views on domestic violence and stops telling women to adjust, accept, and adapt, women will continue to protect the very hand that hurts them.
Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at BRAC Business School and Faizah Zahin is an English and Humanities student, BRAC University.

item.title: On the road again. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
My sister and her retired husband have benefited from forms of support that would be unimaginable in many countries. Assistance with household tasks, social support, and allied health services can help older people and people with disabilities remain at home and maintain a degree of independence.
Australia's aged-care system formally includes services such as social work and physiotherapy among the forms of support that can be provided in home and community settings.
Australia's relatively high wages are another part of this social model. As of July 2026, the national minimum wage is A$26.44 an hour, or A$1,004.90 for a 38-hour week,
Singapore provides another fascinating example.
I spent a couple of weeks there and was struck by what highly educated, pragmatic, and institutionally minded leadership can accomplish when it is combined with administrative competence and a long-term vision.
I visited a school whose principal had become something of a legendary figure. He had grown up poor and had been supported by teachers from religious communities different from his own. His life story was therefore a personal testament to the possibilities of education and merit.
He also played an important role in promoting the recognition of South Asian languages in Singapore's educational system.
Singapore's mother-tongue policy is particularly interesting in this respect. Alongside the country's four official mother tongues -- English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay, and Tamil -- students who meet the relevant criteria can study non-Tamil Indian languages, including Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Punjabi, and Urdu.
The principal told me about an encounter he had with Lee Kuan Yew. He explained that he had argued for the importance of allowing children to maintain a connection with their mother tongue. Lee understood the argument and gave his support.
The principal proudly showed me a copy of the letter, now framed and displayed on the wall of his office.
The episode stayed with me because it illustrated something larger than language policy. A country's development is not simply a matter of GDP, technology, or infrastructure. It is also about whether its leaders understand the importance of education, culture, language, and human dignity.
Travel in the global age may no longer give us the same sense of discovering an unknown world that it once did.
Before the internet, arriving in a distant country could mean entering a world about which we knew very little. Today, Google, YouTube, social media, and satellite television have brought much of the world into our living rooms.
But travel has not become irrelevant. Quite the opposite.
Travel allows us to test what we think we know against what actually exists. It introduces us to people whose lives cannot be reduced to statistics.
It allows us to see institutions at work rather than merely read about them. And occasionally, it offers an insight that is difficult to obtain from books or screens.
In Zadar, the sea itself became an orchestra.
In Croatia, I saw how a small country takes education and sport seriously.
Among Bangladeshi migrants, I was reminded of the distance that can exist between a country's citizens and the people who govern them.
In Australia, I saw how democratic institutions and a welfare state can become part of everyday life.
And in Singapore, I was reminded of the transformative possibilities of education and leadership.
Perhaps, then, the real purpose of travel is not to see places. It is to see societies.
These experiences have left me with one broader thought.
Countries do not develop simply because they possess natural resources, favourable geography, or large populations.
Nor does economic growth automatically produce a just, prosperous, or cohesive society.
Institutions have to be built, maintained, and protected. Schools must function. Public officials must do their jobs. Governments must think beyond the next election. And leaders must understand that public office is a responsibility, not a private entitlement.
Education matters enormously because educated leaders are more likely to understand the complexity of modern societies, appreciate evidence, learn from experience, and recognize the importance of institutions.
But education by itself is not enough. An educated person without integrity can become more dangerous, not less.
Knowledge must be accompanied by honesty, competence, humility, and a commitment to the public good.
The examples I encountered on the road -- from Croatia to Australia to Singapore -- are obviously very different, and none should be romanticized. Every society has its contradictions, inequalities, and failures.
Yet they illustrate a common principle: Development depends not only on resources and policies but on the quality of institutions and the people entrusted with them.
A country needs leaders who are educated enough to understand the world, honest enough to resist corruption, competent enough to turn ideas into institutions, and humble enough to listen to ordinary citizens.
Perhaps that is the most important lesson of travel.
The distance between countries is no longer very great. We can cross it in hours.
But the distance between good governance and bad governance, between competent leadership and incompetence, between public service and self-service, can determine the fate of an entire generation.
And that distance is not measured in kilometres.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Keeping the city clean. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is disconcerting that in Dhaka, a city that generates more than 7,000 tons of waste every day, finding a public bin is still challenging -- a basic gap in public infrastructure that should no longer be acceptable.
The absence of bins makes responsible waste disposal unnecessarily difficult. A pedestrian carrying disposables accumulated through daily activities should not have to walk for kilometres to find somewhere to dispose of them.
While this inconvenience certainly cannot excuse littering, it does highlight the responsibility of the city corporations to provide practical facilities that make good behaviour possible.
There have been attempts before. In 2016, more than 11,000 mini bins were installed across Dhaka, but most disappeared within about a year because of theft and inadequate monitoring.
The fact that the capital is facing essentially the same problem a decade later shows that simply installing bins is not enough.
The current plan by Dhaka South City Corporation to install 2,000 heavier, more durable bins is therefore welcome -- but this time, the authorities must also ensure proper placement, regular maintenance, monitoring, and timely waste collection.
Dhaka North City Corporation, meanwhile, should move quickly to finalize a dedicated roadside-bin program instead of leaving pedestrians without convenient disposal options.
At the same time, public responsibility cannot be overlooked. Bins are useful only when people actually use them, and damaging or stealing public facilities only makes an already difficult problem much worse. Littering should not become the default simply because facilities are inadequate.
Ultimately, this is about more than waste management. Public services should be designed around the everyday needs of citizens, while citizens must also take responsibility for protecting and using those services properly. A cleaner Dhaka will require both.
The city corporations must provide the infrastructure and accountability, and the public must do its part too. Only then can keeping Dhaka clean become a shared responsibility rather than an endless struggle.

item.title: Ensuring the right to healthcare. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain’s declaration that either he or irregularities in hospitals will remain is certainly a strong statement, but the circumstances under which he said so are deeply concerning.
A surprise inspection of Mugda Medical College Hospital was conducted, where the complaints being investigated were unfortunately found to be true -- including that of patients being sent to outside diagnostic centres, despite the hospital having facilities to conduct the required tests.
This is just one example of what is undoubtedly a gross neglect of people's right to healthcare.
Government hospitals are meant to provide accessible healthcare to those who cannot afford expensive private treatment. When patients are directed elsewhere for services that are already available within public facilities, they are not only being made to spend more money, but may also be exposed to unnecessary additional steps and other irregular practices.
The minister also heard complaints about lifts not operating regularly, forcing patients and their relatives to struggle between floors. Such seemingly basic failures can become serious problems for elderly, sick, and disabled patients.
However, impromptu inspections and strong statements can only take us so far. What matters now is what actions are truly taken.
To that end, those responsible for irregularities must be identified and held accountable, while systems should be put in place to ensure such practices cannot simply return once the spotlight moves elsewhere.
This should also be a nationwide effort. If irregularities exist in one government hospital, there is every reason to examine whether similar problems exist elsewhere.
Regular unannounced inspections, transparent complaint mechanisms, proper monitoring of diagnostic services, and consequences for those abusing public facilities can help restore confidence in the system.
Our public hospitals serve millions, often under difficult circumstances. They deserve better management, stronger oversight, and greater accountability.
The minister has made his position clear. Now the health sector needs to see to it that his position is translated into lasting action.

White blazers, pink ties as North Koreans land in Japan for Asian Games. [ dawn ]
item.description:
North Korean athletes wearing white blazers and pink ties were met by pro-Pyongyang supporters waving flags as they began arriving in Japan for the Asian Games on Friday.

More than 100 North Koreans are set to compete in 14 sports at the Games, which take place in Nagoya-Aichi and officially open on September 19.

Nuclear-armed North Korea suspended participation in international sporting competitions during the pandemic but returned at the Asian Games in China in 2023 and also took part in the Paris Olympics.

The smartly dressed men’s football team landed in Osaka on a flight from Beijing at around lunch-time.

North Korea’s flag was prominent on the breast of their immaculate blazers, and they also wore blue trousers and light blue shirts.

They were welcomed by a large group of supporters who sang songs and waved the country’s flag.

The team were presented with bouquets before they boarded a bus and waved from the windows, high-fiving well-wishers.

North Korea’s women’s football team, who have enjoyed stunning international success at youth level, were set to arrive in the evening.

While the Asian Games don’t officially open until next weekend, some events, including football, get under way before then.

The North Korean men open their football campaign against China on September 16.

Their women’s team face Bangladesh on Monday and have been drawn in a group that also includes South Korea, who they will play on September 21.

Japan does not allow North Koreans to enter the country as a sanction for its nuclear and missile development programmes, but exceptions can be made for athletes, said Japan’s chief cabinet secretary Minoru Kihara.

The two countries have no diplomatic relations.

“There are special circumstances warranting an exceptional decision to permit entry,” Kihara said, citing the Games’ aim to foster international exchange.

He reiterated that Japan “in principle prohibits entry by North Korean nationals, and there is no change to this policy”.

A pro-North Korean group in Tokyo has called for people living in Japan to come out and support the athletes.

A video published by Choson Sinbo, a pro-North Korean publication based in Japan, showed students from Korea University explaining how to cheer for teams at the Games.

The smiling students demonstrate chants and songs and urge people to attend events wearing the red of North Korea.

item.title: Bangladesh to develop two new LNG import terminals by 2030. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh plans to commission a new floating storage and regasification unit by 2028 to import liquefied natural gas (LNG), a government minister said on Friday.

Dhaka is also planning to develop a land-based import terminal at Matarbari by 2030, Anindya Islam Amit, state minister for power, energy and mineral resources, said at the LNG Producer-Consumer Conference in Tokyo on Friday.

Bangladesh currently has two floating LNG import terminals, which can regasify up to 1,100 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) of gas.

The new terminal on Moheshkhali Island in the Cox’s Bazar district will have a capacity of approximately 600 mmcfd, while the land-based terminal will have a regasification capacity of approximately 1,000 mmcfd, Amit said, adding that Bangladesh is expanding its LNG infrastructure in anticipation of rising demand for the fuel over the coming decades.

From 2026 to 2030, it will require approximately 3-4 million metric tons per annum (mtpa) of additional LNG, while the additional requirement is expected to increase significantly to approximately 17-18 mtpa between 2031 and 2040, he said.

Bangladesh imported nearly 7 million tonnes of LNG last year, with the bulk of supplies coming from Qatar, according to data from analytics firm Kpler. It has been relying on spot imports this year after QatarEnergy declared force majeure on its shipments after its LNG facilities were damaged amid the US-Iran war.

In July, QatarEnergy halved its scheduled deliveries of LNG to Bangladesh for this year, Petrobangla’s acting chairman Abdul Mannan said, as the fallout from the Iran war curbed shipments of the super-chilled fuel through the Strait of Hormuz.

“All these problems stem from the war,” Abdul Mannan had told Reuters, adding that Bangladesh’s state-owned energy company was exploring alternative LNG sourcing, including more spot-market purchases and government-to-government deals with other suppliers.

In March, as Asia spot LNG prices doubled to three-year highs, Bangladesh reportedly increased its coal power generation and coal-fired power imports, according to daily government data.

item.title: India’s BRICS leadership could offer Bangladesh an economic bridge to recovery. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh approaches the New Delhi BRICS Summit at a critical economic moment. After years of impressive export-led growth and social progress, the country is contending with persistent inflation, slower growth, pressure on its banking sector, and subdued private investment.
The World Bank projects growth of 3.9% in the 2025-26 financial year, while the International Monetary Fund expects consumer-price inflation of around 9.2% in 2026.
Bangladesh is also preparing to eventually graduate from the United Nations’ least-developed-country category. Graduation is a major national achievement, but it brings the challenge of competing without some of the trade preferences that previously supported Bangladeshi exports.
India’s leadership of BRICS offers Bangladesh a bridge between these immediate pressures and its next phase of development. When leaders gather in New Delhi on September 12-13, India will be representing not only one of the world’s largest emerging economies but also the country with the deepest capacity to connect Bangladesh to regional markets, electricity networks, transport corridors, and development institutions.
Bangladesh is not a BRICS member, but it is a member of the New Development Bank. India played a founding role in creating the NDB as an institution capable of financing the priorities of developing economies. Bangladesh’s membership now gives it direct access to an expanding source of infrastructure finance.
The bank is already financing Bangladeshi projects in solar energy and electricity distribution. Its wider discussions with Dhaka cover bridges, railway modernization, urban transit, and maintenance infrastructure. These are precisely the investments Bangladesh requires to restore productivity, attract private capital, and create employment.
Energy cooperation demonstrates India’s role as a regional champion particularly clearly. Bangladesh already imports substantial electricity from India. It has also begun receiving Nepalese hydropower through the Indian grid, creating a historic three-country electricity arrangement.
India’s transmission infrastructure and regulatory cooperation allow clean power generated in the Himalayas to reach consumers in Bangladesh. Bangladesh gains a more diversified electricity supply, Nepal gains export revenue, and India strengthens the resilience of the entire regional grid.
Connectivity provides a second pillar. India and Bangladesh have revived railway links, expanded road connections, and increased the use of inland waterways. The operational use of Chittagong and Mongla ports is creating shorter routes between mainland India and its northeastern states. Bangladesh, in turn, is gaining new opportunities in logistics, port services, manufacturing, and regional commerce.
India’s approach recognizes Bangladesh not simply as a transit route but as an essential economic partner in the Bay of Bengal. Better connectivity increases the value of Bangladesh’s geographic position and helps link its businesses with India’s large consumer market and the economies of Nepal and Bhutan.
This integration matters as Bangladesh prepares for its post-LDC future. The country’s next stage of growth depends on diversifying beyond ready-made garments and moving into higher-value textiles, pharmaceuticals, food processing, electronics, shipbuilding, and digital services. Indian companies, technology networks, and supply chains provide a natural platform for that transition.
India is already emphasizing trade finance, start-up cooperation, resilient supply chains, and support for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. These priorities can complement the growing start-up and digital connections between India and Bangladesh. Affordable finance and easier access to regional markets would help Bangladeshi enterprises expand at a time when domestic credit conditions remain difficult.
Climate resilience is another area in which the two countries’ interests converge. India’s satellite capabilities, forecasting networks, digital public infrastructure, and disaster-management experience add regional capacity to Bangladesh’s internationally respected community-based preparedness.
Cooperation across the Bay of Bengal can improve cyclone warnings, coastal protection, resilient housing, emergency communications, and climate-smart agriculture. The NDB’s focus on sustainable infrastructure gives Bangladesh an additional route for financing projects that protect lives while strengthening economic security.
Neighbours prosper most when connectivity produces balanced benefits. Shared power networks, waterways, railways, and ports create economic interdependence that no country can build alone. India’s size gives it the capacity to initiate these systems.
Disagreements between Dhaka and New Delhi will continue to require patient diplomacy. No mature relationship is free of difficult questions. Yet the architecture of cooperation is now far deeper than any single political moment. Electricity continues to flow, trains and ships continue to move, and development projects continue to connect the two economies.
Rishi Suri is the chief editor at The Daily Milap, one of India’s oldest and largest Urdu newspapers.

item.title: Clock ticking on the Ganges. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Between today and December 12, a narrow three-month window remains for Bangladesh and India to walk the talk on renegotiating and renewing the historic Ganges Water Sharing Treaty. Signed in New Delhi on December 12, 1996, by then Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her Indian counterpart HD Deve Gowda, the milestone 30-year agreement is set to expire at the end of this year.
The Ganges river system -- known as the Padma in Bangladesh -- is a vital lifeline for millions of people, with its basin covering more than a third of Bangladesh’s total land area.
Consequently, there has never been a more urgent need for Bangladesh to ensure that the treaty does not lapse. Anyone in Bangladesh understands how crucial this water is to local livelihoods and how damaging a diplomatic void could be if the 1996 treaty expires without a consensus on renewal or a fresh framework.
While I prefer not to be a naysayer, we are rapidly approaching the deadline with very little visible bilateral discussion. The public is largely unaware of any progress, save for a few stray news reports about technical-level talks and hydrological data sharing.
As someone who has followed Bangladesh-India water negotiations for more than two decades, I find the current atmosphere noticeably lacking in urgency and expediency. With the clock ticking down, the absence of high-level water diplomacy and ministerial-level Joint Rivers Commission (JRC) discussions raises genuine concerns that we might end the year without a fresh deal. I would be glad to be proved wrong.
This quietude stands in stark contrast to the water negotiations in the years immediately after the turn of the 21st century. In the early and mid-2000s, I had the opportunity to observe JRC meetings closely from the sidelines. I watched then Bangladesh Water Resources Minister Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, now the House Speaker, and his Indian counterpart, Priya Ranjan Dasmunsi, engage in fierce but constructive debates.
During the 36th JRC meeting in Dhaka in September 2005, they debated over the Teesta water-sharing formula. Ahmad raised Bangladesh’s genuine concerns about the diversion of Teesta water in the upper riparian region of West Bengal and India’s construction of barrages at Fulertal and Gazoldoba, while Dasmunsi vigorously defended India’s position.
Dasmunsi, a seasoned Congress politician serving in Manmohan Singh’s Union cabinet, was a Bengali born in the Dinajpur region of pre-partition India. I still fondly recall receiving a surprise letter from him in October, 2005, about a month after his visit to Dhaka. In the letter, he was full of praise for the way we gave him a hard time in Dhaka by shooting a barrage of difficult questions.
The beauty of the ministerial talks and subsequent press briefings back then was the complete absence of hard feelings; both sides acknowledged and appreciated each other’s genuine constraints, speaking to the press in a transparent manner without evading even the toughest questions.
Looking back, any water expert in India or Bangladesh can see how pragmatic it was for Bangladesh to sound the alarm over the Teesta in the mid-2000s. We later witnessed how a near-deal in 2011 fell flat because West Bengal’s then chief minister Mamata Banerjee refused to sign an agreement she felt would leave her own state thirsty.
Today, as we push for a timely deal on the Ganges to avoid a legal vacuum, another Indian state has raised its voice. Sanjay Kumar Jha, a prominent Rajya Sabha member representing Bihar, recently called on the Indian government not to renew the Ganges treaty, claiming it has negatively affected his state.
This plea carries significant political weight: Jha was Bihar’s water resources minister as recently as 2024 and currently serves as the national working president of the Janata Dal (United), making him the de facto second-in-command to Bihar Chief Minister Nitish Kumar.
The response from New Delhi was swift. India’s External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar wrote to Jha, assuring him that India would take Bihar’s interests into consideration when deciding on the renewal of the 1996 treaty. While domestic and interstate stakes are India’s internal affair, Bangladesh must take note. We cannot afford to become collateral damage to India’s internal political dynamics. If the ghost of the stalled Teesta deal proves anything, it is that internal roadblocks matter: Back then, it was West Bengal; this time, it could very well be Bihar.
Bangladesh needs to take a cue from the proactive approach of Hafiz Uddin Ahmad two decades ago. Under his stewardship, water talks were conducted in a way that took the wider public into confidence. Whatever discussions are happening today are largely in camera, with very little filtering through to the press.
By contrast, the 35th JRC meeting in New Delhi in late 2003 and the 36th meeting in Dhaka were held under an intense media spotlight. At post-talk press conferences, ministers, delegates, and water experts routinely shared outcomes with reporters, ensuring the general public remained informed. Our delegates debated at length, tackling areas of cooperation alongside major concerns such as India’s river inter-linking project, barrages, and upstream diversions at Tipaimukh, Fulertal, and Gazoldoba.
Beyond the immediate issue of the Ganges, both nations must step up political and ministerial engagement to revive the lost momentum of water diplomacy. If you ask when the two countries’ water ministers last held JRC talks, it is difficult to give an instant answer. Following those 35th and 36th ministerial meetings two decades ago, Bangladesh and India have managed to hold only two more ministerial-level assemblies. This speaks volumes about the gradual disengagement.
In fact, the last time the respective water ministers sat down for a formal JRC meeting was in 2022 -- an event that itself broke a 12-year hiatus. While high-level technical and secretary-level meetings have continued, including the 90th routine technical JRC meeting in May 2026, a fresh ministerial-level assembly has yet to be convened.
The discussion must expand beyond the Ganges alone. Bangladesh needs to swiftly revive the discourse from where former water minister Hafiz Uddin Ahmad left off when he raised serious concerns about India’s inter-linking of rivers (ILR) program. If upstream waters from shared Bangladesh-India rivers are diverted under the ILR project, Bangladesh will face severe water constraints in the foreseeable future.
The scale of this threat was recently underscored by official statements. In a written parliamentary reply last month, India’s Minister of State for Water Resources Raj Bhushan Choudhary said India has formulated a National Perspective Plan for inter-basin water transfer.
Under the plan, 30 ILR projects have been identified, comprising 16 link projects under the Peninsular component and 14 under the Himalayan component. While most of these projects remain at various pre-implementation stages, the Ken-Betwa Link Project has already entered the implementation phase, with a massive budgetary outlay of nearly 45,000 crore Indian rupees.
The project aims to divert 591 million cubic metres of surplus water from the Ken River basin to the water-deficit Betwa basin. Because the Ken flows north into the Yamuna -- the largest tributary of the Ganges -- such large-scale upstream water withdrawal could potentially reduce the volume of water entering the mainstream Ganges.
The consequences extend beyond simple hydrology. A 2023 study published in Nature Communications by researchers at IIT Bombay found that large-scale river interlinking in India alters crucial land-atmosphere feedback loops, potentially reducing summer monsoon rainfall by up to 12% in already water-stressed regions.
Ultimately, these upstream diversions within the Ganga basin could drastically reduce the seasonal flow of the Padma, triggering severe agricultural losses and ecological distress.
The Ganges treaty stands as a testament to the political will that has allowed these two co-riparian South Asian nations to share waters peacefully for three decades. We should be building on this legacy rather than letting it slip away.
Bangladesh and India share 54 common rivers, yet binding instruments, such as agreements or memorandums of understanding (MoUs) exist for only three: The Ganges, the Feni and the Kushiyara. The 2019 Feni River MoU permits India to withdraw a minor 1.82 cusecs strictly for drinking water in Sabroom town, Tripura. The 2022 Kushiyara MoU allows Bangladesh to withdraw 153 cusecs for dry-season irrigation.
Meanwhile, the long-anticipated Teesta treaty, drafted in 2011, remains frozen by West Bengal’s political opposition, while active water-sharing frameworks for seven other priority rivers -- the Manu, Muhuri, Khowai, Gumti, Dharla, Dudhkumar, and Ichamati -- have failed to materialize.
Time is running out. Bangladesh and India must urgently upgrade their diplomatic engagement, bringing ministers back to the table to secure not just the Ganges but the future of the Teesta and the rest of our shared river basins.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: The need for mature cooperation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The reaffirmation of Bangladesh‑India cooperation following the latest high‑level meeting between Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi and Defense Adviser Brigadier General (Retd) Dr AKM Shamsul Islam is a reminder of something both nations often acknowledge but do not always act upon: When Dhaka and New Delhi work together, the entire region benefits.
From trade and connectivity to security and environmental management, the two neighbours are bound by geography, history, and shared interests. Areas of cooperation will continue to be prevalent and relevant. The challenge is to ensure that cooperation is sustained with consistency, trust, and political maturity.
The commitments outlined in the meeting are all practical necessities: Strengthening border management, expanding trade routes, improving energy connectivity, and enhancing people‑to‑people ties. What must be understood is that when cooperation falters between the two nations, it is ordinary citizens that pay the biggest price.
With that said, meaningful cooperation requires maturity -- especially from the larger economy. India, with its size, influence, and regional weight, must show restraint and understanding when grievances arise.
Bangladesh’s concerns over the past couple of years have not been irrational but have stemmed from real issues such as border incidents and delays in resolving water‑sharing agreements, among others. A strong partnership demands that these concerns be acknowledged rather than dismissed.
For cooperation to deepen, India must demonstrate that it values Bangladesh not merely as a neighbour, but as a strategic partner whose stability and prosperity strengthen the entire region.
That means listening carefully, responding constructively, and avoiding actions that create unnecessary pressure. Mature diplomacy is not measured by dominance, but by the ability to build trust.
South Asia is stronger when Bangladesh and India work together. It is in everyone’s best interest that this cooperation not only continues, but evolves with the maturity, restraint, and mutual respect that a true partnership demands.

item.title: Talking about suicide prevention. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With September 10 being World Suicide Prevention Day, Bangladesh must confront a crisis that demands more attention.
Speaking of suicide has always been considered taboo in our society, yet the reality remains that as per the World Health Organization (WHO), Bangladesh records thousands of suicides every year, with an average of about 13 people a day losing their lives. That is a deeply distressing number that must not be brushed aside.
What is even more frightening is that the true scale is likely far higher due to underreporting, stigma, and the absence of a comprehensive national surveillance system.
With women, adolescents, and marginalized communities remaining disproportionately affected, we also lack the mental‑health services needed to help people. Those that exist are unevenly distributed and often inaccessible to those who need them most.
Without coordinated action, preventable deaths due to suicide will only continue. Bangladesh’s current response is nothing if not fragmented, underfunded, and heavily dependent on NGOs. Suffice to say, it is insufficient.
Suicide is a complex issue rooted in mental‑health challenges, economic stress, domestic violence, social isolation, and lack of support systems, to name just a few of the reasons. Addressing it therefore requires a whole‑of‑society approach.
Bangladesh must therefore invest in mental‑health services and integrate suicide prevention into school and community programs while expanding helplines.
Most importantly, we must normalize speaking about mental health and suicide and destigmatize seeking help. Policy-makers must also recognize that suicide prevention is inseparable from broader social protections, from reducing domestic violence to supporting vulnerable youth.
Suicide is preventable, and Bangladesh must ensure real change, real investment, and real protection for those who continue to suffer.

item.title: Your CV is not just a CV. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A CV is usually treated as a piece of paper that helps someone get a job. We write our details, send it to an employer, and move on. But in the digital age, a CV is much more than an application for employment. It is a compact map of a person’s identity. It tells someone where we live, where we studied, where we worked, how to contact us and, sometimes, what we have been doing for years.
That is precisely why the recent controversy over the alleged sale of millions of Bangladeshi job seekers’ CVs on the dark web should worry us far more than an ordinary cyber security incident.
A hacker group calling itself Madrex has reportedly claimed possession of the CVs of around six million users of the popular Bangladeshi job platform BDJobs and has advertised the information for sale. BDJobs has denied the claim.
Yet, 148 CV samples were reportedly published as evidence of the alleged breach. At this point, neither a hacker’s claim nor an institutional denial should be treated as the final word. The important question is not who is telling the truth but whether the public has a reliable mechanism through which such a claim can be independently verified.
This is where our digital culture reveals a troubling weakness. When sensitive personal information is allegedly exposed, the immediate response often becomes a contest of statements.
One side makes a claim, another denies it, and the public is expected to decide whom to believe. But data security cannot be established through public relations. It requires technical investigation and institutional transparency.
If the claim is false, an independent investigation should establish that clearly. If the claim is true, the same investigation should determine how the information was obtained, what information was compromised, and how many people may be at risk.
The larger problem is that we continue to think of personal information as if it were an ordinary administrative resource. It is not. A database containing millions of CVs is potentially a database of millions of identities. Each individual record may contain a person’s full name, telephone number, email address, residential information, educational history, employment history, training and other professional details.
When these pieces are assembled, they become far more valuable than any individual piece of information. A criminal does not need a person’s entire life story. A sufficiently detailed digital profile may be enough to impersonate that person convincingly.
This is where the alleged CV leak becomes particularly disturbing.
A fraudster armed with a person’s professional history can design a much more convincing scam than someone who merely knows a telephone number. A fake recruiter can mention the person’s university, profession, or previous employer. A fraudulent job offer can be tailored to the individual’s career interests. A phishing message can appear to come from an organization the person is likely to trust. The victim may not even realize that the information used to deceive them came from a compromised database.
The European Data Protection Board recognizes identity theft, fraud, and financial loss among the potential consequences of personal data breaches. That understanding is important because it shifts the discussion away from the narrow language of passwords, servers, and firewalls.
The ultimate victim of a data breach is not a database. It is a human being.
A compromised database can be repaired, a password can be changed and a server can be replaced. But once personal information enters the criminal ecosystem, it may be impossible to retrieve it.
If someone steals a document from an office, we understand that something valuable has been taken. Yet when millions of digital records are copied, we often describe the incident as a technical problem. The language itself is misleading. Data theft is theft, even when nothing physical disappears from a building.
The controversy also raises a more uncomfortable question: What responsibility does an organization assume when it collects our information? When people create accounts on job portals, banks, hospitals, universities, or government platforms, they surrender information because they need a service. They do not surrender ownership of their identity.
The organization becomes a custodian of that information, and custodianship creates responsibility. This responsibility cannot end with having a password policy or installing a firewall. Serious data protection requires knowing what information is being collected and why, limiting unnecessary collection, controlling who can access sensitive databases, encrypting information, monitoring unusual activity, conducting regular security assessments, and maintaining a credible response plan.
It also requires knowing what to do when something goes wrong. Security is not a product that an organization purchases once. It is a continuous institutional practice.
The developed world has increasingly recognized this principle. The underlying philosophy is simple: Institutions that collect valuable information must also prepare for the possibility that someone will try to steal it.
Bangladesh needs to develop the same culture of responsibility. Too often, cyber security is treated as the IT department’s problem. It is not. It is a management issue, a legal issue, and increasingly a public-interest issue.
The person responsible for collecting millions of records cannot wash their hands of responsibility by saying that a technical team manages the server. The technical team may operate the system, but the institution carries the responsibility.
There is another reason this particular controversy deserves serious attention. Job seekers are among the people least capable of protecting themselves from the consequences of a data breach. Many are young graduates desperate for employment. They are already vulnerable to fraudulent recruitment, fake interviews, demands for registration fees, and other forms of exploitation. If detailed CV information becomes available to criminals, an already vulnerable group could become even easier to target.
The answer, however, is not to stop sharing information online. Modern life makes that impossible. The answer is to recognize that information has value and therefore demands protection proportional to that value.
We have spent years teaching people to protect their passwords. We now need to teach institutions to protect the information people are forced to entrust to them.
This is ultimately a question of digital dignity. A person should not have to wonder whether the information submitted in good faith to find employment will someday appear for sale in an underground marketplace.
Nor should citizens have to depend entirely on corporate assurances when serious allegations of data exposure emerge. They deserve transparent answers, independent verification, and meaningful protection.
The Madrex claim may eventually prove to be exaggerated, partially true, or completely false. That is precisely why it must be investigated rather than simply argued about.
If the claim is false, an independent investigation can restore confidence. If it is true, the investigation can help identify the breach, protect potential victims, and prevent a recurrence. Either way, the public interest is served by finding the facts.
We often repeat that information is power. But information becomes dangerous when it is concentrated in the hands of those who have no right to possess it. The real lesson of the alleged CV leak is not that hackers have become more dangerous. It is that institutions entrusted with our information must become far more responsible.
A CV may help someone get a job. But in the wrong hands, the same CV can help someone steal a person’s identity. We need to understand that difference before the next six million records become another statistic.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Time to clean up our polythene problem. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to intensify action against the unchecked use of polythene and plastic should not be treated as another routine instruction.
Polythene bags, single‑use plastics, and unregulated packaging have been a major reason for our environmental degradation. The reality has been clogged rivers and drainage systems to contaminated farmlands and wetlands to plastic piling up in urban neighbourhoods with little to no attempt to fix any of it.
We must also recognize that the unchecked use of plastic also contributes to urban flooding, destroys ecosystems, contaminates soil, and adds to the public‑health burden.
That polythene has been banned in Bangladesh for well over two decades now, yet the ban exists only on paper, is what is particularly infuriating. Once again, we already recognize the issue and have the law in place but unfortunately, enforcement has been non-existent and plastic consumption has grown unchecked.
This lack of accountability and disregard that has unfortunately come to define our nation must no longer be tolerated and as such, the prime minister’s words must be treated as a turning point.
Bangladesh cannot aspire to be a middle-income nation while allowing polythene and plastic to undermine every aspect of environmental management.
The government must act decisively. Start with shutting down illegal polythene factories and enforcing fines on distributors. They must also ensure that alternatives -- jute bags, biodegradable packaging, and regulated plastics -- are not only widely available but are a viable alternative for the masses.
Bangladesh has long had the policies, the laws, and the public awareness that polythene and plastic damage our nation. What it has lacked is consistent enforcement and political will. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has made the call and the country must now respond with urgency and discipline.
A liveable Bangladesh will always be out of reach if polythene and plastic continue to choke our rivers and streets. It is time to clean up.

item.title: A senseless tragedy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has now crossed a devastating milestone in its measles outbreak, with the death toll reaching 1,000 -- a number that represents a thousand families mourning children who should have had every chance to grow up.
Measles is, while highly contagious, also a preventable disease through timely vaccination, and that makes this tragedy even harder to accept.
The outbreak has exposed dangerous gaps in the country’s immunization system. Routine vaccination programs were disrupted during a period of political upheaval, while subsequent problems with vaccine procurement further weakened protection.
The result has been an immunity gap that left hundreds of thousands vulnerable.
It must be understood: There can be no justification for allowing political disagreements, administrative transitions, or changes in policy to interrupt essential healthcare services.
Children cannot be made to wait for stability while governments change, political priorities shift, or institutions are reorganized. A missed vaccination today can and has become a life-threatening infection tomorrow.
It is therefore imperative that the government treat routine immunization as a national priority that must remain independent from political turbulence. Vaccine procurement and distribution need stronger oversight, adequate stockpiles and clear accountability.
The health authorities must also maintain reliable records to identify children who miss doses and ensure that the missed vaccination reaches them.
The emergency vaccination campaign was necessary earlier this year but it cannot be the end of the response. Bangladesh must rebuild a resilient immunization system capable of functioning through subsequent crises.
Public awareness must also improve so that parents understand the importance of timely vaccination and know where to obtain it.
Most importantly, there must be accountability. 1000 child deaths cannot simply become another statistic in an annual health report.
Political disagreements must never again come at the cost of preventable infant deaths. In fact, no preventable disease should be allowed to claim a single child’s life because the systems meant to protect them failed.
We owe our children this much.

item.title: Why the government should prioritize regional economic development, and now. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has been given three more years for LDC graduation. The UN Committee for Development Policy has recommended deferring our graduation from least developed country status to November 24, 2029. The General Assembly is due to take the decision before November this year.
The Committee attached a condition in its own words, that the extension should not be viewed as an opportunity to delay reforms but should accelerate them. The question that follows is a plain one: What are the three years for?
My answer is regional economic development, and I do not mean it as a matter of fairness between divisions. I mean it as the fastest route we have to a diversified export base, to jobs at the scale the country needs them, to women's employment that does not require a woman to move house, and to growth that adds less to the environmental load we already carry.
We usually pursue these as four programs with four budgets. But they meet in one place, which is the region.
By regional development, I do not mean spreading projects more evenly across divisions. I mean treating a division as an economic unit with a declared specialization rather than as an administrative area that receives its share of everything. That has four parts: (i) each division carries a declared economic identity based on what its enterprises already do best; (ii) public investment there is sequenced to that identity instead of spread thinly across every sector; (iii) the support functions the identity needs, being finance, standards, testing, skills and logistics, are built at the cluster rather than in the capital; and (iv) one institution is answerable for the division's economic outcome and is measured on it.
The first part should not be difficult, as our productive geography is already specialized. The specialization is also sharper than our policy acknowledges. In the agro-logistics system mapping we undertook for the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands this year, we found that the top three mango producing districts account for roughly 50% of national output, and the top three papaya districts for 43%. Watermelon has been shifting into Patuakhali, Bhola, and Barguna, where the top three districts now hold around 30%.
The pattern holds well outside agriculture. Bogura carries around 70 foundries and 1800 manufacturing and workshop units. These meet some 70% of national demand for agricultural machinery and spare parts, are worth Tk500 crore a year, and employ about 15,000 people. Bhairab in Kishoreganj holds over 10,000 shoe making units across some 20 villages. The trade there supports close to two lakh people and turns over Tk15-20 crore a day.
None of this was planned. These are comparative advantages that enterprises built themselves, and no policy has yet been written to them.
Writing one would look concrete, and it would look different in each place. Rajshahi would be developed as a horticulture economy. The packhouses, hot water treatment plants and phytosanitary certification that mango and papaya exports require would be sited there rather than at the airport in Dhaka.
Bogura would be developed as a light engineering economy. It would need metallurgical testing, tool and die capability, industrial training, and working capital lines, as these are what let a foundry district move from spare parts into finished machinery it can sell abroad.
Bhairab would be developed as a footwear economy, with component supply, design services, and the standards testing that an international buyer asks for before placing an order.
Each of these is a different economy and each needs a different set of institutions. That is not what we build.
What we build is one national system, and we build most of it near the capital. Our logistics costs stand at 15-20% of the GDP, which is amongst the highest in Asia. This cost falls hardest on the production areas that are farthest from the capital. Nearly 95% of our cold storage is dedicated to potatoes.
Producers of fresh vegetables are thus forced to send their produce fast to urban markets. The highways cut travel times to those markets by 30-40%, but did not address the issue of preservation. We lose 6.0-8.1 million metric tons of cereal a year, worth $2.1-2.8 billion. A 30% reduction would save $630-850m and feed 15-20m people without bringing another hectare into cultivation.
The environmental case is not separate from this. We have little new land or water to bring into cultivation. Additional food will therefore have to come from what we stop losing.
Activities that we will require to overcome this loss would also push the frontiers for jobs. Grain spoils as nobody dried, graded, or stored it, and that work would be employment. Agriculture contributes about 11% of GDP but employs 43-44% of the labour force. Most of our workforce is thus in the part of the economy that produces the least value per worker.
Only around 12% of our agricultural output is processed. The work that would close the gap is drying, chilling, grading, packing, machining, assembly, and stitching. It belongs in the cluster rather than in Dhaka.
This matters most for women. Our garment industry brought women into waged work, but it required them to move to Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj, and Chittagong. The move cost them in the form of rent, travel, and separation from their families. Work sites at the cluster do not ask that price, as they are available where women already live and where their labour is often already offered without wages. A quarter of the Bogura light engineering workforce is already made up of women, despite the fact that it was not designed to employ women.
The question therefore is, why does economic development remain centralized? It is because we are yet to have the institutional system to support regional development. There is no institution that owns a region's economic outcome. Our Annual Development Program is allocated by ministry and by project, never by region. Nobody is therefore answerable for what Bogura's or Barishal's productive base looks like in five years.
The Local Government Division takes the largest share of the ADP and carries no economic development mandate. We have already tried the alternative of announcing sites. Of the 100 economic zones announced, roughly a tenth reached the ground in a decade before the program was cut back to five.
A zone is a site. A site with neither an owner nor a declared purpose fails to become an economy.
Other countries in the Global South have given their regions an owner, and I have watched this at close quarters in the work I do outside Bangladesh. In Nigeria, every state carries a declared economic identity. Lagos is the Centre of excellence and Kano the Centre of commerce. Those declarations came first, and the instruments were built to them afterwards, most recently Lagos's industrial policy and the state-level agro-industrial processing zones.
The declaration is what made the investment legible to everyone who had to act on it. Vietnam supplied the piece that Nigeria does not, which is measurement. Its Provincial Competitiveness Index gives every province a published score on economic governance, and provinces compete on it openly. We have neither the declaration nor the score.
Both are available to us within the current fiscal year. The FY2026-27 Annual Development Program is Tk3 lakh crore, 30% above last year. It already names region-based balanced development amongst its five pillars, with the northern region, the coastal belt, Chittagong, and Mongla named specifically.
The intent is on paper and the money is appropriated. What is absent is the machinery.
The government should declare an economic identity for each division on the comparative advantage its enterprises have already built. It should name a single owner for that identity within the Planning Commission. It should then publish a divisional measure the owner is held to.
Tk74,000 crore of this year's ADP sits in block allocation, undirected; that is the instrument. Routing it through the divisional plans would cost nothing that has not already been budgeted.
How this should be done -- meaning the sequencing, the institutional design, and the financing -- needs more space than a column allows, and I will set it out separately. What I am arguing here is the prior point: The decision to organize the economy regionally has to be taken in this fiscal year for any of that design to matter. Three years is not long for this kind of work. If we begin in the next budget rather than this one, we will reach November 2029 with the structure half built and the preferences gone.
The Committee for Development Policy was right that the extension is not an opportunity to delay. It is the time available to build in, and what we should build is regional.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director, Innovision Consulting.

item.title: The invisible plastic problem we can no longer ignore. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For years, the public face of plastic pollution has been easy to recognize: Bottles caught in rivers, shopping bags on roadsides, wrappers buried in rubbish dumps. But increasingly, attention is turning to particles so small that they can pass unnoticed through everyday life.
In Bangladesh, that concern has recently entered an unexpectedly familiar place: The bathroom. A July 2026 study by the Environment and Social Development Organization, or ESDO, reported that microplastic particles were detected in 26 of 34 toothpaste samples tested from local and imported brands.
The findings have prompted concern among consumers and drawn the attention of policy-makers, with the High Court ordering an expert investigation into the matter.
The study does not establish what those particles mean for human health, nor does it suggest that every plastic-containing product presents the same risk. But it has raised a larger question: How much plastic do we encounter without thinking about the material itself?
A material question
Modern packaging is built around convenience. It protects food from contamination, keeps clothes clean during transport, and allows products to travel thousands of kilometres before reaching a customer.
Plastic became central to that system because it is inexpensive, light, and durable. Those same qualities, however, create a problem when the product reaches the end of its useful life.
A bag used for a few minutes can remain in the environment for years. As larger plastic items weather and fragment, they can produce particles commonly referred to as microplastics.
That has changed the way environmental researchers and policy-makers think about plastic pollution. The question is no longer simply whether a package performs well. It is also what happens to its material after it has performed its job.
There is a potential solution. Bangladesh's apparel industry is one of the country's defining economic forces. It also produces an enormous quantity of something that receives considerably less attention: Textile waste.
Every garment factory generates scraps. Some are reused or recycled. Others have little economic value and can become a disposal problem.
That discarded material can be used to produce compostable packaging, including shopping bags, grocery carriers, apparel packaging, and mailer bags. There are already companies that have started doing this.
The conventional packaging system is largely linear. Raw materials are extracted. Products are manufactured. Packaging is used. Then it becomes waste. Circularity attempts to interrupt that sequence. Materials are kept in productive use for longer, recovered where possible and, where appropriate, returned to natural or industrial cycles.
Compostability is not simply a claim that a material will “disappear”. The conditions under which a product breaks down, the testing method used, and what remains afterward are all important parts of the scientific assessment.
This is where the recent toothpaste findings intersect with a much wider debate. The concern around microplastics is not confined to toothpaste. Researchers have reported their presence across a range of environmental and consumer settings, while scientists continue to investigate how these particles move through ecosystems and what their long-term implications may be.
But the response cannot simply be to declare every plastic product dangerous. The more useful question is one of material design. If packaging is made from a material intended to persist, then its environmental fate must be considered over a long period. If packaging is made from a material designed to compost, then its environmental fate is different.
The most important part of a package may be the part that nobody sees. Not the logo. Not the colour. Not the handle. The end. A conventional plastic package is designed primarily around its useful life. Its environmental fate comes afterward, often outside the control of the manufacturer or consumer. A circular approach tries to consider that fate at the point of design.
There has to be more to a biodegradable or compostable shopping bag. It is an argument about responsibility. What should happen to a material when its job is finished? Should it persist? Should it be recycled? Should it be reused? Or can it safely return to the biological cycle? There will not be one answer for every product. But increasingly, companies are being asked to provide an answer.
The environmental movement has spent decades asking people to produce less waste. The next phase may require something more difficult: Rethinking what we call waste in the first place. A discarded piece of fabric has already absorbed energy, labour and resources. Treating it as worthless at the end of one production cycle ignores the value still contained in the material.
The recent toothpaste findings have brought an invisible form of plastic pollution into an unusually intimate setting. That may be uncomfortable. But perhaps discomfort is useful when it makes a familiar system worth questioning.
The issue is bigger than toothpaste. It is bigger than shopping bags, too. It is about whether the materials we design today are suited to the world we expect to live in tomorrow.
For Bangladesh, that conversation has an additional dimension. A country whose economy has been built in part on textiles is now experimenting with ways to turn textile waste into another industry's raw material. That is more than waste management. It is an attempt to redesign the relationship between production and disposal. And perhaps that is where the next packaging revolution will begin.
Tarif Mohammad Khan is a brand marketing, business strategy, and communications expert.
