item.title: From a Pandemic Era Peak to a Cautious Recovery. [ daily-sun ]
Explained: Why is everyone so mad about Karachi province?. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Talk of Pakistan’s territorial reconfiguration is back in circulation again with mention of the division of Sindh producing the most bile.

It was all started by the interior minister who told businessmen in Islamabad last month that he mourned the collapse of Pakistan’s “outdated governance system”. Urgent reforms were needed, he argued, if Pakistan wanted to avoid blowback from “cockroaches” (Gen-Z agitating in India). Our salvation lay in the decentralization of governance which could be achieved by creating new administrative units (read: provinces).

People who make a case for new provinces argue that the existing ones are too large to manage and there is too much distance between the government and the people. Smaller units would be more efficiently governed and would thus bring the seat of power closer to the people.

Some commentators took his remarks rather seriously and started to earnestly do the math, running numeric options for a new ‘right-sized’ and reconfigured Federation of Pakistan: 5, 8, 10, 12 provinces, depending on which flavour of administrative reform you liked. South Punjab, Greater Karachi, Seraiki province, Hazara province. And secretly everyone wondered if the minister’s rhetoric had wafted down from the rarefied exosphere of the supra-political elite.

Three groups have made their preferences clear over the question. The Establishment seems to be in the mood for ‘right-sizing’ the state. Political parties have expressed mixed views. And nationalist parties, particularly from Sindh, have opposed it.

Sindh has been the angriest. Its house of elected representatives passed an unequivocal resolution against any proposal to change the boundaries of the province. What explains this reaction and what is the history to this sentiment?

Desh-making

When Partition took place, Sindh had already operated as a fully-fledged province for a decade after it was separated from Bombay in 1936. And with independence in 1947, it regained the old feeling of distinct territorial existence which it had experienced before the arrival of the British in 1843. This rejuvenated consciousness tinged with pride of belonging to one of the oldest civilizations in the world, the Indus Valley, made Sindhis particularly sensitive to their restored ethno-territorial identity.

That is why today you cannot mention a ‘Karachi province’ without picking the scab off a very old wound.

Partition caused the first injury in 1947 when it shook the foundations of Sindh’s demography and power structure. In a blink of an eye, its middle class mainly made up of Hindus emptied out as they fled to India and were replaced by Muhajirs coming from India. And then the federal government decided to take Karachi as the country’s capital, strip it of its provincial capital status and name Hyderabad instead. This was the catalyst for Sindhi nationalism, which went on to challenge the new State’s national project by insisting on ethnic identity and territoriality.

Meanwhile, the second injury to the identity of Sindh came in the shape of One Unit (1955). With the stroke of a pen, the federal government created the two provinces of East and West Pakistan to establish what was at best an artificial parity between the two wings of a country. The creation of a mega province in West Pakistan was a disaster as it gave rise to resistance in the shape of ethnic nationalisms in the three minority provinces of Pakistan. Suppression of the sub-national identity of language as a primordial loyalty of people led to a fully-fledged nationalist movement in East Pakistan.

Not surprisingly, the National Awami Party as a representative of Pakhtun and Baloch nationalisms and the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) as a representative of Sindhi nationalism formed governments in these provinces after the 1970 elections (and creation of Bangladesh in 1971). The message was clear. You tinker with ethnolinguistic identity, you give rise to a tsunami of mass mobilization.

Spearheading this agitation were the famous ‘sons-of-the-soil’ such as G. M. Syed, Ibrahim Joyo, Shaikh Ayaz and Rasul Baksh Paleejo. Finally, after twenty years of mass resistance, General Yayha was obliged to undo the decision and make Karachi the capital of Sindh back again in 1970, and bring an end to the One Unit.

The late 1970s onwards, Sindh has stood out from the other provinces because it has had unique competing nationalist movements. In fact, Sindh remains the most ethnically polarized province of Pakistan, making the question of territorial reorganization all the more difficult to grapple with. Muhajirs have strongly reacted to policies such as the 1972 declaration of Sindhi as an official language, a 60:40 quota for civil service and educational institute admissions favouring rural Sindh and the nationalisation of industries and universities.

Thus the PPP and Sindhi nationalist groups sit at one end of the opinion spectrum and the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) at the other.

Each player’s position

Massive ethnic outbidding between the PPP, the MQM and the Sindhi nationalists is taking place with the latter including offshoots of G. M. Syed’s Jeay Sindh Mahaz. While these parties have not dominated at the ballot box, they represent the spirit of Sindhi nationalist consciousness and act as an important pressure group on the PPP as a frontline actor in the domain of governance.

The PPP has been in power in Sindh since 2008. It is a coalition partner in the ruling dispensation in Islamabad. Since its inception, it has been able to connect Sindhis to the state through its electoral success. It has been able to present Sindh’s grievances at federal platforms such as the Council of Common Interests and National Finance Commission Awards to split funds among the provinces. It oils the security mechanism of the interests of Sindh within and beyond the provincial boundaries.

The Sindhi nationalist parties have, however, focused on identity construction through grassroots politics. They are weak electoral entities but their influence on shaping Sindh’s imaginary is strong. For instance, their opposition to the 2012 Local Government Act that introduced a separate local bodies system in Karachi compelled the PPP government to re-think its policy. In early 2025, a controversy erupted with the proposed construction of canals in south Punjab that would have diverted water away from Sindh. Under mass public pressure, the PPP government was obliged to listen to the nationalist parties.

Meanwhile, the MQM has learnt that it can never be in a dominant position in Sindh due to its demographic limitations at one-fourth of the population. Since 1988, it has been a coalition partner of several governments and it has generally looked towards Islamabad for support. It has been unhappy with the empowerment of provincial governments through the 18th Amendment because this means more power in the hands of the provincial majority Sindhis at the cost of the largest minority of Muhajirs.

These misgivings aside, however, the promise of devolution remains unfulfilled almost a decade and half after the passage of the amendment. Provincial governments have avoided transferring administrative and fiscal powers to local governments. The limited powers of local governments have grossly alienated the MQM. On several occasions, this party has demanded a federal takeover of Karachi in the name of good governance and efficient service delivery.

How could it be done legally?

Article 239 (4) of the Constitution says any change in the territorial make-up of a province needs the approval of two-thirds of a provincial assembly as well as the National Assembly and the Senate. In today’s divided political landscape, it seems impossible.

This is why a referendum has been mentioned as a way to acquire ‘popular’ consent for smaller provinces. The history of referendums and their like conducted in Pakistan by the military governments of Ayub, Zia and Musharraf does not, however, inspire much confidence especially as they were rigged.

What people are really scared of

The proposed division of Sindh has galvanized shades of public opinion. The nationalist parties opted for street mobilization. The PPP led the passage of a resolution in the Sindh Assembly. It seems that the creation of new provinces will have the most catastrophic consequences for Sindh. One frightening scenario is a population transfer that invokes the memory of 1947. Since Muhajirs are concentrated in urban centers, they might decide to migrate to a Muhajir-majority province (if created). This would lead to cross-migration across the boundaries steeped in blood. Indeed, it would give rise to a storm of discontent in all parts of Sindhi society, beyond the Sindhis and Muhajirs. Is the State ready to handle such a storm?

item.title: Steeped in bad economics. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Tim Worstall says Bangladesh's tea estates should die because they can't pay market rates for capital. He built that on a price that was, for years, not a market price at all: Whatever a small pool of buyers felt like paying that week, with no floor underneath.
In 2023, Bangladesh produced a record 102.9 million kilograms of tea, while the corresponding auction year delivered a 12-year low average price of Tk171.24 per kilogram. Then the Bangladesh Tea Board introduced minimum auction pricing.
By 2025-26, the average auction price had risen to Tk245.50, up 43% -- and total auction revenue had increased by roughly Tk562 crore, even though less tea was sold through auction.
That's a broken pricing mechanism, not a verdict on tea.
Everything else in his argument rests on that price being honest. It isn't, and the rest of this piece works out the consequences.
I come to this from both sides; I studied economics and political science, have come from a family that has grown tea for four generations, and work in venture capital for emerging and frontier markets.
I've watched capital wasted propping up businesses that should have died. Worstall isn't wrong to worry about that. He's wrong about where the disease sits.
A tea estate is not a spreadsheet
My favourite economics joke: Assume rationality. Frictionless markets, perfect information, the model hands you the answer you wanted before you built it.
That's Worstall's picture -- capital and labour gliding from tea to whatever earns more this quarter.
Bangladesh's tea sector employs roughly 102,000 permanent workers and 40,000 seasonal ones. Close to half a million people live inside estate boundaries.
These are not abstractions to me. Factories my family has run, land my grandfather planted, and my father and uncles have managed. There are names and faces I know behind those numbers.
An estate isn’t just tea bushes. It includes housing, schools, roads, water systems, embankments, farmland, factories -- none of it fungible.
A tea company is not the same as any other factory or office. It’s a strange combination of agronomy, microeconomics, political systems, and many things hard to explain in a single article, best explained over a few cups of tea and a long afternoon. Anyway, I digress.
What I mean is that an estate doesn't deserve to survive simply because people depend on it. But exit has a cost, and it lands on people, not a balance sheet.
The sleight of hand
A 6% loan when inflation runs at 8% is concessional financing. Fine. But Worstall treats a subsidy's existence as proof of what it's used for.
That doesn't follow: Bangladesh's own garment industry was built on duty-free imports, bonded warehouses, and tax holidays before it became the country's largest export earner.
Some subsidized spending is waste. Some are why an industry exists at all. A subsidy tells you nothing about which bucket you're in. The real question is what the concession buys.
Another year of losses with nothing changing is a slow bleed with a government signature on it -- fair criticism. But financing replanting, irrigation, or debt restructuring is transition capital. Priced correctly, that's how you fix things.
There's a second case for keeping capacity alive that has nothing to do with restructuring math: Import substitution. Bangladesh's domestic tea consumption has been closing in on production for years, and the country already imports tea most seasons to cover the gap.
Every estate that goes under doesn't just cost jobs and export earnings; it widens a shortfall the country then has to fill in foreign exchange.
That's not a reason to keep a terminal estate on life support. But it is a reason the value of a marginal estate can't be read off the auction price alone.
Now the receipts
Once the Tea Board introduced a minimum price to correct that twelve-year low, the average price rose by roughly Tk74 per kilogram within two years, adding hundreds of crores in producer revenue -- without a single bush growing better tea.
When the Board pushed the floor further, buyers boycotted an auction outright, leaving more than half the tea offered unsold that day.
The price was never an unimpeachable verdict on value. It was the output of a lopsided buying process, and the buying side had enough leverage to walk away from half a season's output rather than pay more.
What the price actually measured was leverage, not tea.
Between the producers and the retail shelf sits a long chain -- brokers, blenders, packeters, whoever finally puts a brand name on the box -- each taking a cut. Ordinary commodity economics, not a scandal.
But it means the auction price captures only one point in a much longer chain, with no guarantee the margin is split fairly between growers and everyone downstream.
If an estate can't produce tea at a cost the market will sustainably bear, that's structural, and Worstall's remedy applies.
If it produces something worth far more than it's paid, but the value leaks out between garden and shelf, that's a market failure -- and closing the garden doesn't fix a market failure. Fixing the market does.
The test that actually matters
None of this means every estate survives -- that would be as lazy as Worstall's conclusion. Some will need restructuring more radical than a rate cut can provide, some need new ownership or a different use for the land. Let the evidence decide, estate by estate.
So far it doesn't look terminal: Production hit 95 million kilograms in 2025, against a record 102.9 million in 2023, the same year prices bottomed out. A sector producing more than ever and getting paid less than ever for it -- a margin problem, not a dead one.
There's a real difference between "a business with no credible path to viability should exit" and "needing concessional financing proves a business destroys value." The first is analysis. The second is an assumption wearing analysis as a costume.
The task force behind this financing paired it with replanting, export strategy, and debt restructuring. Cheap credit without reform is life support; tied to performance, it's a turnaround.
Estates that can't show a credible path shouldn't get it indefinitely. On that, Worstall is right.
The right test: Can this estate become productive and sustainable? Where yes, finance the transition and measure results. Where no, let the capital move.
Less satisfying than "things that lose money should close down." But having spent a career on the investing side of exactly this question, I'll take the answer that's actually correct.
Farhan A Rahman is the founder of Lontana Consulting, an emerging-markets advisory firm, and a fourth-generation tea planter. He is obligated to have an opinion on tea economics.

item.title: A directive is not a river cleaned. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On September 6, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman convened a review meeting at the Secretariat on pollution control across the Buriganga, Turag, Dhaleshwari, Balu, and Shitalakhya.
He told the room that citizens should not simply wait for government orders but must act out of personal responsibility to protect these rivers.
It is the right sentiment and the right rivers. But responsibility cannot be the answer to a problem this paper's own reporting has already quantified.
Five days earlier, Dhaka Tribune published the findings of a BIWTA survey that should be sitting on every desk at that review meeting: 424 identified discharge points pour roughly 330 tons of waste into the Buriganga, Turag, Balu, and Shitalakhya every single day.
Industry accounts for nearly 60% of it. Of the 424 outlets, 244 trace back to private factories and industrial units.
That is not a diffuse crisis of collective habit. It is a mapped, countable, addressable set of pipes.
And that is precisely why the directive-and-appeal approach that dominated Monday's meeting will not move the number.
For two decades, Dhaka has treated industrial river pollution as a law-and-order problem: raids, fines, and closure notices. The BIWTA survey shows what that approach has produced -- a system still discharging at full volume, just better documented.
The reason is structural, not a failure of will. More than 30,000 industrial units -- dyeing, washing, tanning, textile finishing, chemicals -- sit across Hazaribagh, Tejgaon, Shyampur, Gazipur, Narayanganj, Keraniganj, and Savar, most of them small and medium enterprises operating as subcontractors on margins of 5-10%.
A functioning effluent treatment plant for a mid-sized dyeing unit costs $150,000 to $400,000 to build, plus steep monthly costs for power, chemicals, and skilled operators.
For an owner at that margin, bypassing the ETP is not defiance. It is how the business survives the season.
The government is not positioned to police its way past that arithmetic. Jurisdiction over these rivers is split across the Department of Environment, RAJUK, Dhaka WASA, BIWTA, the city corporations, and the Ministry of Industries -- a structure in which everyone has a mandate and no one has full accountability.
The BIWTA survey itself illustrates the fragmentation: 66 WASA drains feeding directly into the Buriganga and Turag, 21 outlets under Dhaka South, 16 under Dhaka North, 37 under Narayanganj, plus union parishad drains scattered across Kutubpur, Zinjira, Kalindi, and Shakta.
Each belongs to a different authority. None of them, alone, can close the river's pollution loop. Add an informal economy of unregistered subcontracting units invisible to any inspector, and the familiar cycle repeats: Drive announced, fines issued, and factories shuttered for a week, then quietly reopened.
This is why the PM's call for "collective effort" needs to be pointed at the state's own machinery before it is pointed at citizens.
Three shifts would matter more than another enforcement drive.
First , stop asking 30,000 individual units to each build a compliant ETP; no industrial economy has cleaned its rivers that way.
The proven model is the common effluent treatment plant (CETP), and Bangladesh already has the cautionary tale it needs: The Savar Tannery Estate's CETP was built, then operated poorly.
The lesson is not that CETPs fail -- it is that the government must treat operation, not just construction, as its job, ideally by contracting professional operators under performance-based, transparently-monitored agreements.
Second , make compliance financially possible before demanding it. Bangladesh Bank's green refinance schemes rarely reach the SMEs that most need them.
A targeted package -- low-interest loans for ETP and CETP connections, duty waivers on treatment machinery, a phased subsidy covering 40–60% of CETP connection costs for the first three years, and a tariff structure that charges pre-treating factories less -- would convert compliance from a cost worth evading into infrastructure worth using.
Third , pair regulation with capacity-building: ETP design clinics with BUET, BGMEA, and BKMEA; certified training for operators; a simplified online clearance process; and public, river-zone-wise disclosure of compliance data, so that export buyers already sensitive to green standards do enforcement the state cannot.
None of this excuses the factories dumping into the Buriganga today. The polluter-pays principle should stand. But paying assumes a service exists to pay for, and in most of these clusters, it does not.
Monday's meeting reviewed activities "already undertaken." The BIWTA survey is the evidence of where those activities have gotten us: A fully mapped, still-flowing 330 tons a day.
The rivers do not need another appeal to conscience. They need the ministries in that Secretariat room to build the CETPs, unlock the financing, and coordinate the jurisdiction they already share on paper.
The PM is right that people should not wait for directives. The state should not wait either -- it now has the map.
Ahad Chowdhury, PhD, is a geologist and environmental scientist.

item.title: Protecting small businesses from extortion. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest reporting on extortion in Dhaka’s markets reveals a crisis that has gone on for far too long and one that must be taken seriously.
Small traders are the backbone of our capital’s daily economy but are being squeezed by criminal groups, politically-connected operatives, and local strongmen who demand payments simply for the “right” to operate.
At a time when everyday people are struggling due to numerous economic challenges, that these small traders and businesses are having to experience this is distressing, to say the least.
That a systematic pattern of intimidation exists that is draining livelihoods, raising prices for consumers, and eroding public trust in law enforcement should alarm the authorities and compel them to take action with immediate effect.
Many traders pay because the alternative is violence, vandalism, or being forced out of business entirely. Some have already shut down operations, unable to survive the pressure.
We must also recognize that this is not merely a law‑and‑order issue but also an economic threat. When small traders are extorted, the entire supply chain suffers. Prices rise, competition shrinks, and honest businesses lose ground to those protected by criminal networks.
Authorities cannot pretend this is invisible any longer. Enforcement remains sporadic, and crackdowns rarely dismantle the networks behind the extortion. We agree with experts on the matter that a few arrests will not solve a problem that is deeply entrenched.
What is needed is a sustained, uncompromising campaign against extortion. Police must protect traders, not leave them to negotiate with criminals while market committees must be held accountable when they enable or ignore illegal collections.
Most importantly, we need our political leadership to make it clear that extortion will be met with decisive action and not just empty promises.
Small traders keep Dhaka running and they have earned the right to safety, dignity, and the freedom to work without fear. It is time for the authorities to prove that the city belongs to its citizens, not to those who prey on them.

item.title: Preserving our harvest. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The near‑completion of a modern cold storage facility in Bandarban is undeniably good news. Farmers lose large portions of their seasonal fruits and vegetables every year due to inadequate storage in our country. To combat this loss, cold storage facilities are nothing if not a lifeline.
However, there is a truth we cannot deny: Bangladesh needs many more such facilities, and it needs them fast.
Bangladesh’s farmers have long been forced into distress sales, watching their produce spoil before reaching the market. A 50‑metric‑ton cold storage, now 95% complete, will certainly go a long way to help preserve their harvest and potentially reduce post‑harvest losses, protect incomes, and give growers the confidence to expand cultivation.
For a district with enormous untapped potential, this could be transformative for its farmers.
However, the fact is that Bangladesh’s agricultural infrastructure remains very uneven. In too many districts, farmers still rely on makeshift sheds, improvised cooling, or no storage at all. As a result, bumper harvests often turn into financial disappointment.
We may speak of boosting exports, diversifying crops, and strengthening food security, but without modern storage facilities, these ambitions remain fragile.
The Bandarban facility should therefore be seen as the beginning of a nationwide push to modernize post‑harvest infrastructure.
Every major producing district needs cold storage that matches its output. Farmers deserve to have access to reliable preservation so they are not forced to sell at throwaway prices every year.
For a robust future where we can tackle growing threats of food security, it is simply not enough to depend on what our farmers can grow. We must be able to preserve our harvest.

item.title: On London's Brick Lane, a data centre sparks local battle. [ dawn ]
item.description:
In Brick Lane, the historic heart of London’s Bangladeshi community, residents oppose plans for a data centre in a disused brewery, citing the erosion of heritage and need for social housing.

“This has really been the focal point of the British Bangladeshi community,” local councillor Faysal Ahmed told AFP, recalling a time when his parents ran a restaurant beneath his childhood home in the Lane.

While many curry houses remain, the street and the surrounding neighbourhood is transforming, in part to help power the capital’s digital infrastructure boom.

Part of a multi-million pound redevelopment of the sprawling former Truman brewery site, the East End financial data centre is an unlikely addition to the graffiti-lined Brick Lane, where tourists spill between vintage shops and queue for bagels served through the night.

The 10-acre site will also be transformed by new offices and retail space, primarily serving the neighbouring financial district filled with skyscrapers.

Approval of the development by the UK government comes as a boom in water- and energy-hungry data centres — particularly as demand rises for facilities supporting artificial intelligence — fuels local opposition worldwide.

For Ahmed, the development uses land that could help house some of the roughly 31,000 residents on the waiting list for social housing in the Tower Hamlets district.

The redevelopment plans are for only 44 flats, including just six for social housing, prompting residents to recently protest outside the Ministry of Housing.

‘Preserving heritage’

“My personal concern is about the need for affordable social housing for young people and preserving the heritage, the special character, of the area,” said Susanna Kow, a member of the Save Brick Lane campaign.

According to planning documents, the Labour government gave “significant weight” to the benefits of additional data centre capacity, citing the need to “meet the escalating demand driving emerging technologies such as AI and increased digital services”.

The government’s housing department declined to comment on its decision in August to approve the plans, while the Truman Brewery has not responded to an AFP request for its reaction.

“We’ve been campaigning on planning issues and… the incursion of the city on the East End for quite a number of years,” said Jonathan Moberly, who is leading local opposition.

He said the project was part of a “growing national issue about the amount of power taken from the grid that can stop other developments happening, like housing”.

The International Energy Agency in April reported that the global electricity demand of data centres grew by 17 per cent last year.

It projects the electricity consumption from these centres will double over the next five years to 2030.

“The UK already faces a projected daily water deficit of nearly five billion litres by 2050,” according to a report on the UK government website.

“National water resource plans… do not adequately account for the burgeoning demand from infrastructure such as AI data centres. This oversight risks intensifying water stress in already vulnerable regions.”

‘Trojan horse’

For industry consultant Mark Acton, the infrastructure is increasingly essential, particularly in London, a city where proximity can provide the ultra-fast response times needed for financial trading.

“Everything we currently do digitally comes from a data centre,” said Acton, who argued the facilities have become an easy target owing to what he said was a lack of understanding of their actual water and energy use.

If Britain is serious about sovereignty over its AI infrastructure, “you’ve got to have somewhere to put it”, Acton said.

But campaigners at environmental charity Global Action Plan argue that UK planning rules have not kept pace with the expansion of the sector or adequately accounted for environmental costs.

“It’s been a kind of Trojan horse for bad development,” Owen Espley, the group’s community campaigns manager, told AFP.

“We need local knowledge and input to go into shaping developments to improve them and make sure that we get better data centres at the end of it,” he said.

Further down Brick Lane, Carol Burns, born and raised in the area, has no intention of going anywhere.

Sitting inside the shop her family has run since the 1800s — its walls covered with family photographs — Burns is proud to be part of London’s East End community.

“People are always trying to buy this place, but no. They’ll have to drag me out of here feet-first,” she said in her thick Cockney accent.

item.title: The India–China reset will continue at the BRICS summit. [ chathamhouse ]
item.description:
The India–China reset will continue at the BRICS summit Expert comment jon.wallace 8 September 2026

So will disagreement over the purpose of BRICS.

India will host the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September at a time when the rest of the world is increasingly seeking to emulate its longstanding policy of strategic autonomy.

The Ukraine and Iran wars, continuing US–China rivalry, and the second administration of President Donald Trump have made New Delhi’s long-held commitment to strategic hedging and middle power diplomacy seem wise, if not urgent underpinnings for modern international relations.

However, even though the world may better reflect India’s worldview, New Delhi has found it difficult to apply its foreign policy approach to its BRICS chairmanship. 

Strain with Washington, reengagement with Moscow and Beijing

Recent Indian government actions confirm India’s continuing commitment to strategic hedging. New Delhi secured a string of resource deals during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent visits to Australia, Indonesia and Uzbekistan. And it has agreed a number of trade deals, with nine in-progress or concluded since 2021 – including with the United Kingdom and European Union.

Trade negotiations with the United States continue, but relations with the second Trump administration have undoubtedly been strained, causing India to reinvest in other relationships.

Ony a few years ago, India was distancing itself from the China-led Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO): New Delhi hosted a low-key virtual summit in 2023. And Modi was absent from the summit in 2024. But more recently India has renewed its interest in the grouping and sought to improve relations with China and Russia. At this year’s SCO summit, Modi joined President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin in signing the Bishkek Declaration, which condemned US-Israeli military attacks on Iran.

India’s BRICS agenda

India has consistently sought to be a ‘voice’ of the Global South, often by using its prominent position in platforms like the G20 (which it chaired in 2023) and the AI Impact Summit (which it hosted earlier this year).

Its BRICS chairmanship has continued these efforts. In August a joint declaration, the ‘Chennai Consensus’ made a commitment to collaborative research and innovation among developing countries on emerging technologies. The same month, BRICS trade ministers advocated preserving and revitalizing the multilateral trading system – a move likely aimed at the Trump administration’s disruptive tariff policies. And in June, BRICS agriculture ministers issued a food security declaration focused on the needs of developing countries.

The challenge for New Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-Western but not explicitly anti-Western. To that end, it has sought to downplay some of the more controversial elements of the BRICS agenda. That includes a de-dollarization narrative championed by countries such as Brazil and Russia – an idea which last year caused President Trump to threaten to slap ten per cent tariffs on the BRICS in response.

Related work

How China–India relations will shape Asia and the global order

New Delhi emphasized that BRICS is not seeking to create a separate reserve currency to compete with the US dollar. It has instead reframed this as an effort to settle bilateral trade in national currencies and use digital payments to reduce transaction costs for cross-border trade.

India has also promoted a more benign worldview, reflected in the BRICS slogan of ‘Humanity First’ and the theme of ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’. But this seems increasingly outdated given recent geopolitical developments, in particular US military action against Venezuela and Iran.

India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-Western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other BRICS countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high profile diplomatic disputes with the US.

A key watchpoint at this summit will therefore be how New Delhi reconciles its efforts to stay on good terms with Washington with calls by BRICS member states to voice opposition to US actions. As Chair and host of BRICS, India’s actions will be more scrutinized, and it will be reluctant to oversee the production of a statement similar to Bishkek. 

Multilateral symbolism

These tensions are exacerbated by the broader challenges of maintaining cohesion among the 11 BRICS member states. Tensions between Iran and the UAE, for instance, are high as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Relations between Addis Ababa and Cairo have been strained by Ethiopia’s Nile dam project. Saudi and UAE interests conflict on relations with Israel and other issues. And India has its own longstanding frictions with China to manage, although there have been signs of improvement over the last two years.

Additionally, among the founding member states – Brazil, Russia, India, and China – there is still no consensus on what the BRICS stands for. Brazil and India see it primarily as an economic-driven initiative. China and Russia see it through more of a geopolitical lens. Beijing in particular is increasingly using forums like the BRICS to promote its own worldviews through its Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives. Meanwhile, Moscow has used the BRICS to seek alignment with the Global South as it is ostracized by the West following its invasion of Ukraine.

From New Delhi’s perspective, BRICS has been moving in the wrong direction. BRICS was established as a reaction to calls for a greater voice for the Global South in multilateral institutions, with a focus on development and governance. India would like to build on the organization’s earlier achievements, including the establishment of the BRICS New Development Bank and Contingent Reserve Arrangement in 2015.

The difficulties BRICS has speaking with one voice could affect its future. In the two decades since the BRICS was formed, newer groupings have emerged, such as the recent defence pact between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. There is a possibility that such regional, exclusive groupings may become more important actors than expansive and inclusive groupings like BRICS.

Such factors mean that BRICS expansion is likely to take a backseat for the foreseeable future. Instead, the focus will probably be on socializing new members into the organization.

Efforts to expand the BRICS mandate will likely be limited to engagement with other forums in the Global South. However, even this is challenging. Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rehman – whose country holds the chair of BIMSTEC, a South and Southeast Asian regional forum – has not yet accepted an invitation amid tensions with India.

Bilateral substance

The real action at the BRICS Summit will take place on its sidelines with a series of bilateral meetings. In particular, the meeting between Modi and Xi is likely to further advance the ongoing reset in bilateral relations and build confidence. A meeting in August between the Chinese foreign minister and Indian national security advisor made notable progress on their longstanding border dispute. And Xi’s upcoming visit to India – his first since 2019 – will reportedly include a 400-person delegation.

In this context, the recent accomplishments of BRICS have come from its convening power. It was a Modi–Xi meeting at the 2024 BRICS Summit in Russia that set the ball rolling on resetting the relationship.

Ultimately, the Global South remains an amorphous concept. There remains little clarity on what advocating its interests actually means, beyond making vague calls for a more equitable distribution of power in a multipolar global order. The BRICS summits needs to move behind platitudes and statements towards more substantive outcomes if it is to be seen as a real contender in global governance.

At the summit, New Delhi will seek to return BRICS to its original development-focused agenda, as reflected in its Economic Partnership Strategy 2030. However, this threatens to be hijacked by fissures among its members and calls for another statement condemning US attacks on Iran. But the group needs more than opposition to the US to define a better vision for the Global South. This entails moving beyond what it stands against to what it stands for.

item.title: Bangladesh’s literacy future begins before first grade. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On the 60th anniversary of International Literacy Day, Bangladesh stands at an important point in its education journey. According to the Bangladesh Sample Vital Statistics 2023: Key Findings report, the national literacy rate among people aged seven and above rose to 77.9%, from 58.6% in 2014.
Yet these gains do not tell the whole story. Functional literacy, the ability to read, write, think critically, and apply knowledge in daily life, remains out of reach for millions.
According to the World Bank’s Human Capital Index 2020, 58% of 10-year-olds in Bangladesh are unable to read and understand a simple text by the end of primary school.
That is more than one in every two children.
One important part of this challenge begins even before children enter primary school.
A study by Nirmala, Umayahara, Yang and Ranganathan (2021) shows that up to 80-85% of children from the poorest socioeconomic quintiles enter Class 1 without adequate pre-literacy exposure, structured storytelling, or formal early childhood education.
When children enter primary school without these foundations, they are expected to cope immediately with a fast-paced curriculum. This can lead to early frustration and poor comprehension.
Children from disadvantaged backgrounds are three times more likely to drop out of primary school than their wealthiest peers. This, in turn, can reinforce an intergenerational cycle of poverty and weaken the country’s human resources.
The gap is even wider for children with disabilities. They often face multiple barriers, including negative attitudes, delayed enrolment, and a lack of adapted learning materials. These obstacles can exclude them from the literacy journey before it has properly begun.
Children do not all learn and develop at the same pace or in the same way. Using fixed developmental milestones to decide whether a child is “ready” for school can unfairly disadvantage children with disabilities. Yet with appropriate support, every child can learn and participate.
Early lessons from the GPE KIX- and IDRC Canada-supported EN-REACH Education implementation research project, being conducted in selected government primary schools in Kushtia and Gaibandha districts, suggest that school readiness cannot be strengthened by focusing on the child alone.
The support surrounding the child, particularly from teachers, parents, and other caregivers, also matters.
Preliminary qualitative findings suggest that children with disabilities who were initially shy or anxious became more confident and engaged when they experienced language-rich, play-based learning at home and in school.
Teachers also reported that inclusive, play-based approaches designed to support children with disabilities benefited other children in the classroom as well.
The research is also showing the value of equipping pre-primary teachers with practical skills for inclusive teaching and of using low-cost, locally-available play materials.
At home, involving fathers, grandparents, and community members in school-readiness activities can broaden responsibility for early learning and help build a more supportive and gender-equitable environment for children.
These emerging lessons point to a wider conclusion: Inclusive pre-primary education works best when the classroom, home, and community reinforce one another, rather than when school readiness is treated solely as the responsibility of the child or teacher.
But promising approaches in a few settings will not be enough unless quality pre-primary education becomes more widely accessible. Across Bangladesh, access to quality early education remains deeply unequal.
First , Bangladesh needs to invest more in early education. Expanding preschool enrollment in low- and middle-income countries could generate benefit-to-cost ratios ranging from 6.4 to 17.6.
Yet Bangladesh spends just over 2% of GDP on education, well below Unesco’s recommended 4% to 6%. A significant, protected share of increased education spending should go to pre-primary education in marginalized communities.
Second , inclusion and play-based learning need to become central to pre-primary education.
Classrooms should have age-appropriate reading materials in children’s mother tongues, interactive toys, and storybooks. Pre-primary education should also move away from excessive memorization and give children more opportunities to learn through play, stories, interaction, and exploration.
Third , the pre-primary workforce needs to be professionalized. Teaching young children, particularly children with disabilities, requires specialized pedagogical skills. This should receive proper attention in education planning, budgeting and implementation.
Finally , evidence-based inclusive models need to be scaled up. As stronger evidence emerges on effective ways to include children with disabilities and engage fathers in early learning, the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education, the National Curriculum and Textbook Board, and development partners should consider how these practices can be incorporated into national policy.
If Bangladesh wants a population capable of succeeding in a digital economy, participating meaningfully in society and escaping poverty, investment must begin when the human brain is developing most rapidly.
By ensuring universal, high-quality, play-based and inclusive pre-primary education for every child, Bangladesh can make sure that improvements in literacy are not simply reflected in statistics, but in the knowledge, skills and opportunities of its people.
Utpal Mallick is an Assistant Program Manager at icddr,b and can be reached at utpal.mallick@icddrb.org .

item.title: From a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar to New York University. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
When I fled Myanmar in 2017, I carried very little with me. My family escaped violence, persecution, and fear.
We walked for days through forests and mountains before reaching Bangladesh. Along the way, we lost our home, our security, and the future we had imagined.
But there was one thing I refused to leave behind: My belief in education.
Today, on World Literacy Day, we often think about literacy as the ability to read and write. For refugees, it means much more.
Literacy can mean understanding your rights, accessing reliable information, communicating with the world beyond a refugee camp, challenging misinformation, and finding the confidence to speak for yourself.
For me, education became one of the most powerful forms of protection.
As a Rohingya refugee in Bangladesh, I watched thousands of young people grow up with extremely limited access to formal education. They had dreams of becoming doctors, teachers, engineers, lawyers, and community leaders.
Displacement did not take away their talent or ambition. It took away their opportunities.
This distinction matters.
Refugees do not choose to become refugees. No child chooses to flee war, persecution, or violence. Yet once displaced, refugee children are often expected to carry the consequences of decisions they never made.
They encounter restrictions on movement, lack of legal documentation, poverty, discrimination, language barriers, and limited pathways to higher education.
The result is not simply an education crisis. It is a loss of human potential.
When a young person spends years in a refugee camp without meaningful access to education, we should not ask why that person has failed to progress. We should ask why the systems around them failed to provide an opportunity.
I know what that feels like.
For years, I tried to find a way to continue my education while living as a stateless Rohingya refugee in Bangladesh. There were moments when the possibility of attending a university seemed almost impossible.
I had the desire to learn. I was willing to work. What I did not have was the legal status and opportunity that most students take for granted.
Yet I continued.
In 2024, after seven years as a refugee in Bangladesh, I came to the United States as a student. This year, I graduated from New York University with a bachelor's degree in social science, concentrating in international studies.
My journey from a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar to a university classroom in New York has taught me something important: Talent is universal, but opportunity is not.
I am not the only Rohingya young person capable of reaching a university. There are students in the refugee camps today who could become doctors, lawyers, teachers, entrepreneurs, researchers, diplomats, and leaders.
But talent cannot substitute indefinitely for access.
Through the Rohingya Student Network, which I founded while living in the refugee camp, I have seen what happens when young people are given opportunities to learn.
Education does more than transfer knowledge. It builds confidence. It develops leadership. It gives people the tools to understand the forces shaping their lives and the ability to participate in decisions about their future.
That is why literacy should also be understood as a question of power.
A person who can access information, evaluate it critically, understand their rights, communicate their ideas, and tell their own story is harder to silence.
For a stateless community whose identity and history have repeatedly been denied or misrepresented, that matters enormously.
Literacy also matters in the digital age. Refugees increasingly receive news, communicate, organize, study, and understand events through phones and social media.
Being literate today therefore requires more than reading words on a page. Young people must also be able to distinguish information from misinformation, understand how digital platforms influence what they see, and use technology responsibly.
For the Rohingya, these skills are particularly important. We have already witnessed the devastating consequences of misinformation, hate speech, and dehumanizing narratives.
Education must therefore prepare young people not only for employment but also to think critically, challenge hatred, engage peacefully with others, and become responsible participants in their communities.
The international community often speaks about durable solutions for refugees. Education must be at the centre of that conversation.
Investing in refugee education is not charity. It is one of the smartest investments governments, universities, and donors can make in human potential.
Educated refugees contribute to economies, strengthen communities, promote social cohesion, and help build peace.
They become problem-solvers rather than being viewed solely through the lens of humanitarian need.
My life changed because people and institutions eventually saw beyond my refugee status and recognized my potential as a student. That should not be an exceptional story.
On this World Literacy Day, I hope we move beyond asking how many refugee children can read and write. We should ask a much bigger question: How many have been given the education necessary to determine their own future?
Food keeps people alive. Shelter provides safety. Humanitarian assistance helps people survive displacement.
But education gives people the tools to move beyond survival.
For a refugee, a book can be more than a book. A classroom can be more than a classroom. And literacy can be more than the ability to read and write.
It can be the beginning of freedom.
Maung Sawyedollah is a Rohingya student and activist currently living in New York City. He graduated from New York University this spring with a BA in social science and is currently preparing to start a JD.

item.title: Beyond the banana raft: Asadul’s story and the road to better education in chars. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
During the monsoon period, going to school was never just a simple walk for Asadul.
The books in his schoolbag often became wet. The muddy path between home and school turned slippery and treacherous. A deep canal stood between his home and the classroom, and when rain came, it swelled into a strong current.
Sometimes he waded through waist-deep water. On other days, he crossed on a raft made of banana trees.
Yet he kept going.
For a boy growing up in the remote char village of Nowshala in Kurigram's Chilmari upazila, school represented something much greater than a classroom. It was a pathway to a different life.
From an early age, Asadul dreamed of becoming a doctor -- a dream that appeared almost impossible in a place where even reaching school became a daily struggle.
Today, that boy is a student at Rangpur Medical College.
His journey is extraordinary, and it also speaks to a much larger reality in Bangladesh.
Over the past decades, the country has made significant progress in bringing children into school. About 97% of primary school-aged children were enrolled in school, while the dropout rate declined significantly from 40% in 2010 to 13% in 2023.
But, for those living in remote and climate-vulnerable areas, the harder challenge is often staying in school, completing secondary education, and finding a pathway to higher education.
Bangladesh has made steady progress in expanding access to education, but significant gaps remain in remote char areas.
The Bangladesh Education Sector Analysis 2026 highlights persistent “last mile” challenges, high dropout rates, and continuing disparities affecting children from low-income households, remote and vulnerable areas, and other marginalized groups.
Asadul's life offers a human face to those statistics.
When he was growing up, there was no school in the vicinity of Nowshala, surrounded by the Brahmaputra River. For the communities, education remained beyond reach.
That began to change in 2006, when Friendship established a primary school in the area. Asadul enrolled in 2008.
He was still young, but he had already seen the harshness of char life.
River erosion repeatedly threatened his family's home and land. Poverty was a constant reality.
Yet while the river could take away land and possessions, it could not take away his determination to study.
"During floods, I sometimes crossed the canal on a banana raft. Often my books and notebooks got wet," Asadul recalls. "But I always felt that if I stopped going to school, my dream would disappear too."
It is difficult to imagine what those words meant to a child who had to negotiate floodwater simply to attend class. But for Asadul, education had already become inseparable from his hope for a better future.
Photo of Asadul at Rangpur Medical College. Photo: Courtesy
After six years of struggle, he completed primary education. Yet the next stage proved even more difficult.
There was still no nearby secondary education opportunity. To continue studying, Asadul had to leave home and depend on others.
He stayed in different households, taught their children, and did household work in exchange for food and accommodation. He also worked in hotels, agricultural farms, and crop-processing centers.
His education was sustained not by comfort, but by sacrifice.
"To continue my studies, I had to move from one house to another. In return, I taught their children and did different kinds of work, he says."
The arrangement was not always kind.
"Sometimes families demanded money for food and accommodation, which I could not afford. I had to leave those places and start again elsewhere. There were days when I worked in other people's homes just to arrange one meal."
Still, he refused to abandon his education.
"I always carried a dream -- to become educated, change my destiny, and bring happiness to my family and society."
His daily routine was grueling: Classes during the day, work in the afternoon and evening, and study late into the night.
Eventually, he completed both secondary and higher secondary education.
Then came the medical admission test.
For Asadul, becoming a doctor had never been simply about choosing a profession. It had become a personal promise -- to himself and to the family whose hardships he had witnessed since childhood.
Guidance and encouragement from mentors helped him gain confidence about higher education and career choices. He began studying 14 to 15 hours a day.
But his first attempt at the medical admission test ended in regret. He missed the opportunity by just two marks.
For many students, such a narrow margin of failure could have ended the dream. For Asadul, it became another reason to try.
The following year, the result he had waited for finally arrived.
In the 2022–23 academic session, Asadul secured admission to Rangpur Medical College.
The distance he had travelled was not merely geographical. It was a journey from a place where a child once had to cross floodwater to reach a primary classroom to a point where that same child could enter one of the country's prominent medical colleges.
"Every night before going to sleep, I feel that I am finally becoming a doctor," he says. "In the future, I want to serve disadvantaged people as a compassionate physician."
His words carry a significance beyond personal achievement.
Bangladesh's education story is often told through enrollment figures and examination results. But behind those numbers are children whose educational journeys are shaped by where they are born, whether their families can afford to keep them in school, whether a road remains passable during the rainy season, and whether they can see a future beyond the next examination.
The challenge is particularly acute in climate-vulnerable communities.
Unicef says children living in disaster-affected parts of Bangladesh are among those most at risk of exclusion from school.
In 2024 alone, climate-related events disrupted the education of 35 million children in Bangladesh, with heatwaves, cyclones, and floods causing repeated school closures and, in some areas, children losing up to eight weeks of learning.
For children in the chars , education must mean more than opening the door of a school. It must mean creating a continuous pathway -- from primary education to secondary school, from secondary school to higher education, and eventually from education to dignified work and meaningful participation in society.
The support of educational initiatives and career guidance can help students from remote communities see possibilities that may otherwise remain invisible.
Asadul’s story is ultimately about what a young person can do when opportunity meets determination. Yet stories like his suggest that something else is changing in Bangladesh’s chars.
As access to education expands, children are beginning to imagine futures as doctors, engineers, teachers, and other professionals.
It reminds us that talent does not belong only to cities, nor does ambition stop at the edge of a river.
This is the larger promise of education in Bangladesh: Not simply getting children into classrooms, but enabling them to stay, learn, progress, and aspire.
Building a better Bangladesh therefore requires more than expanding access. It requires resilient schools and learning opportunities in vulnerable communities, stronger support for children at risk of dropping out, quality learning, pathways from primary to secondary education, career guidance, and opportunities to continue into higher education.
The boy who once crossed floodwaters on a banana raft is now on his way to becoming a doctor.
His story is not only about how far one child has travelled. It is about how far Bangladesh can take its children if education reaches the last mile and the pathway does not end there.
Sometimes, building a better future begins with simply helping a child reach school. The real transformation comes when that child is given the opportunity to keep going.
Ruhul Kuddus is the General Manager of the Education Sector, Friendship.

item.title: Ensuring remittance keeps trending upwards. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is encouraging to find that remittance inflows have reportedly increased by 18.6% to $6.05 billion in the current fiscal year, especially at a time when the country continues to navigate economic pressures and needs stronger foreign-exchange earnings.
Remittances have long been one of Bangladesh’s most dependable sources of foreign currency while also providing vital support to millions of families, so the latest growth deserves recognition.
More importantly, this should encourage policy-makers to build on the factors that are helping formal remittance channels become more attractive and accessible.
For a country with a large overseas workforce, there is considerable room to do more: Migrant workers make enormous sacrifices to earn abroad, and ensuring that their hard-earned money can be sent home safely, quickly, and at reasonable cost should be a priority.
Globally, the cost of sending remittances remains significant, with the World Bank reporting an average cost of 6.36% across the corridors it tracks, and Bangladesh must continue working to reduce such costs.
At the same time, the government and financial institutions need to maintain policies that encourage migrants to use official channels. Better exchange rates, simplified procedures, stronger digital services, and greater confidence in the banking system can help sustain the upward trend while reducing reliance on informal methods.
But increasing remittance inflows should not become an excuse for complacency. Bangladesh must ensure that these foreign earnings contribute to broader economic stability and productive investment in long-term economic security rather than merely meeting immediate consumption needs.
The latest figures are undoubtedly positive; they demonstrate the continuing contribution of Bangladeshis working overseas and offer some much-needed momentum for the economy.
Now, we must keep the focus on making formal remittance channels even easier, protecting migrant workers’ interests, and creating an environment where every dollar sent home can generate maximum value for families and the country alike.

item.title: Literacy must mean more. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As we observe International Literacy Day today, it is important to remind ourselves that literacy is not merely the ability to read and write but a fundamental human right and a foundation for accessing wider knowledge, skills, and opportunities.
Yet, it is disheartening that despite decades of progress, at least 739 million young people and adults worldwide still lack basic literacy skills.
For Bangladesh, this remains a particularly relevant concern. The country has made significant strides in expanding access to education, particularly among younger generations: Unesco data put youth literacy at 93.4%, while literacy among those aged 25-64 stands at 76.1%.
These figures show both how far Bangladesh has come and how much work still remains.
More importantly, literacy cannot be treated as a statistic that ends once someone can sign their name or read a sentence. In an increasingly digital society, people must be able to understand information, distinguish fact from misinformation, navigate technology, and also apply what they learn to everyday decisions.
This is especially important in Bangladesh, where access to digital services, financial systems, healthcare information, and government services is rapidly expanding.
The challenge here is twofold: Ensuring that children receive strong foundational literacy and reaching adults who were left behind by the formal education system.
Rural communities, disadvantaged families, older people, and those living in climate-vulnerable areas deserve particular attention.
Encouragingly, Bangladesh already has examples of innovative approaches, such as Sidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha’s solar-powered floating schools, which received Unesco’s Confucius Literacy Prize.
The government must build on such initiatives rather than treating literacy as a campaign-day issue. Better-funded adult education, stronger foundational learning, trained teachers, and accessible digital-literacy programmes are essential.
On this International Literacy Day, Bangladesh should remind itself that literacy is not simply about producing people who can read. It is about empowering citizens to understand, participate, and prosper -- and that must remain the ultimate goal.

item.title: What you can do to combat dengue. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is no longer facing dengue as a simple seasonal disease. It has evolved into a complex public health challenge influenced by climate change, rapid urbanization, environmental degradation, changing human behavior, and weaknesses in vector control systems.
The alarming rise in dengue cases over the past several years clearly indicates that traditional approaches are no longer sufficient. Dengue prevention and control must now be viewed as a national development priority rather than merely a health-sector responsibility. The changing epidemiology of dengue in Bangladesh demands a fundamental shift in strategy.
Climate change isn't just altering ecosystems but actively reshaping infectious disease boundaries and elevating the spillover and epidemic risks of neglected, rare pathogens. Climate change has significantly altered the pattern of mosquito-borne diseases worldwide, and Bangladesh is among the countries most vulnerable to its consequences.
Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, prolonged monsoon seasons, waterlogging, floods, and increasing humidity have created ideal conditions for the breeding and survival of Aedes mosquitoes. Previously, dengue transmission was largely concentrated between June and September. However, recent outbreaks have demonstrated that the transmission season has expanded beyond traditional boundaries.
Unpredictable weather patterns are allowing mosquitoes to reproduce more rapidly and survive for longer periods. Urban flooding creates countless artificial breeding sites, while warmer temperatures accelerate both mosquito development and viral replication.
Therefore, climate change adaptation strategies must be integrated into Bangladesh's dengue control policies. Public health authorities should collaborate closely with meteorological agencies, urban planners, environmental experts, and local government institutions to develop climate-informed dengue forecasting models.
One of the greatest misconceptions in Bangladesh is the belief that fogging alone can control dengue.
Fogging primarily targets adult mosquitoes and often provides only temporary relief. However, Aedes mosquitoes reproduce in small collections of clean, stagnant water found inside homes, on rooftops, in flowerpots, in discarded containers, on construction sites, in water storage facilities, etc.
The most effective intervention remains the destruction of mosquito breeding sites. Vector control should become a year-round activity rather than an emergency response implemented only after case numbers begin to rise.
Dengue control ultimately depends on human behavior. The Aedes mosquito is predominantly a household mosquito and breeds in domestic environments and usually bites during the daytime.

Unfortunately, many people continue to view dengue prevention as the sole responsibility of city corporations. This mindset must change. Behavioral change communication should become a continuous national campaign.

Instead of conducting indiscriminate insecticide spraying, resources should be directed toward identifying mosquito breeding hotspots through entomological surveillance and geographic information system (GIS)-based mapping.
Integrated vector management also requires close coordination among the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, city corporations, municipalities, educational institutions, the Ministry of Local Government, the Department of Environment, and urban development authorities. Dengue is not simply a medical problem; it is an environmental and governance challenge.
No country has successfully controlled dengue without active community participation. Community engagement should move beyond awareness campaigns and evolve into community ownership. Neighborhood-based clean-up campaigns, school health programs, youth volunteer initiatives, and community surveillance teams can significantly reduce mosquito breeding sites.
A nationwide weekly "Dengue Clean Day" could become an effective public health intervention. Local communities should be encouraged to inspect their homes and surroundings regularly and report potential breeding sites to local authorities. Bangladesh's own dengue strategy recognizes community participation as the key to sustainable dengue control.
Rapid and often unplanned urbanization has transformed many areas of Bangladesh into favourable environments for Aedes mosquitoes. Blocked drainage systems, indiscriminate waste disposal, plastic containers, abandoned tires, rooftop water accumulation, and poorly managed construction projects continue to create ideal breeding habitats. Environmental sanitation should therefore become an integral component of dengue prevention.
Priority actions should include:
The responsibility for environmental sanitation extends far beyond the health sector. Urban planners, engineers, municipal authorities, construction companies, and communities must work together to reduce environmental risks. Bangladesh's current guidance specifically highlights waste management and sanitation as critical components of dengue prevention.
Every year, hospitals become overwhelmed when dengue cases begin to surge. This reactive approach must be replaced by proactive preparedness.
Institutional readiness should include:
Health facilities should begin preparing before the onset of the monsoon rather than waiting for patient numbers to increase. Early diagnosis and appropriate case management remain the most effective ways to reduce dengue-related deaths. These preparedness measures are also emphasized in national recommendations.
The World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends the use of the dengue vaccine Qdenga® (TAK-003) for children aged 6-16 years living in areas with high dengue transmission intensity.
Importantly, vaccination should never replace traditional prevention measures. WHO clearly states that dengue vaccines should be implemented as part of a comprehensive dengue control strategy.
One of the most important lessons from recent dengue outbreaks is that surveillance systems must become more predictive.
Traditional case reporting alone is insufficient. Bangladesh requires an integrated early warning system that combines:
A modern surveillance system should identify high-risk areas before outbreaks occur rather than simply documenting cases after transmission has already intensified.
Effective surveillance can provide policy-makers with the information needed to deploy resources, strengthen vector control, and prepare health facilities in advance. National strategies already emphasize real-time reporting, hotspot mapping, and early warning systems.
Bangladesh continues to repeat the same mistake every year by initiating dengue control activities after the arrival of the monsoon. This approach must change. Seasonal preparedness should begin at least two to three months before the rainy season and include:
Dengue control activities should follow an annual preparedness calendar rather than an emergency response model. Current guidance recommends that control activities begin before the peak transmission season.
Bangladesh has successfully addressed many major public health challenges through strong political commitment and multisectoral collaboration. Dengue should be approached in the same way.
The country needs a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach that brings together:
The fight against dengue requires behavioral change, environmental responsibility, scientific surveillance, climate adaptation, institutional preparedness, and community ownership.
Dengue is no longer merely a seasonal outbreak. It is a warning signal about the intersection of climate change, urbanization, environmental neglect, and public health vulnerability.
Dr M Salim Uzzaman is a public health specialist & strategist (expert: EIDs, disease surveillance, One Health, and global health security).

item.title: Labuschagne makes the cut for Australia Test squad for South Africa. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne can “still make a positive contribution”, chief Australia selector George Bailey said on Monday, after the struggling batsman was thrown a lifeline for the Test tour of South Africa.

Number three Labuschagne has failed to score a century since 2023, and flopped again in two home Tests against Bangladesh last month with scores of one, 31 and four.

He was subsequently axed from Australia’s squad for three One-day Internationals in Zimbabwe and another three in South Africa preceding the Tests.

But selectors opted against a red-ball change for what will be the team’s first Test series in South Africa since the infamous “Sandpapergate” ball-tampering scandal in 2018.

“(We’re) not shying away from the fact that we’d like some more runs from Marn… but we’re also confident that he can still make a positive contribution to that squad,” Bailey said.

“Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn’t been functioning as successfully as we would like.” Asked if the South Africa series would be Labuschagne’s last chance, Bailey dodged the question.
“No, I wouldn’t say that. But again, it’s a hypothetical, isn’t it?” he said.

Cooper Connolly, Matthew Kuhnemann and Michael Neser were also included in a 16-man squad which was otherwise unchanged form the last Bangladesh Test.

All-rounder Connolly’s selection is another indication that the 23-year-old is seen as a long-term prospect while Kuhnemann was preferred to Todd Murphy as the second spinner behind Nathan Lyon.

Neser, who like Labuschagne was born in South Africa, provides back-up for the pace trio of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc.

Bailey said Connolly was primarily chosen for his batting, most likely as a middle order option but potentially as high as three.

“His overall development will continue to expand his ability to bat in a range of positions,” he said.

Australia travel to Durban for the first Test on October 9 before the series moves to Gqeberha and Cape Town.

Only Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood, Lyon, Steve Smith and Matt Renshaw survive from their last Test series in South Africa, when Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were all sent home in shame.

Smith was banned for a year and sacked as captain after conspiring to alter the ball using sandpaper during the third Test in Cape Town, while the now-retired Warner, considered the ringleader, was suspended for 12 months and stripped of all leadership roles.
