item.title: Makkah Defense Alliance: Should Bangladesh step into the quicksand?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
After World War II, military alliances emerged in various regions as a result of the ideological competition between the Western world and the Soviet Union. But in today’s world, there is no longer competition between two distinct camps, and many regions have no such military alliances.
That is perhaps why the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement has aroused curiosity in many countries. The geographical composition of the Makkah Alliance and the circumstances surrounding its formation have given rise to considerable speculation.
The formal journey of this alliance, comprising Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, began a month ago. On September 1, at the first formal meeting in Istanbul, it was decided to establish a secretariat in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia.
At the same time, the military and diplomatic leaders of the three countries decided to appoint a Pakistani official as the alliance’s first secretary general for a three-year term.
Following the political decision to form the alliance, the process of establishing its administrative and management structure is now beginning. The easier tasks will come first.
It is expected that the more complex steps required to make a military alliance effective will be taken in the future. However, beyond those complex steps, much remains to be determined -- including the alliance’s ideology, objectives, policies, expansion, and identification of enemies and allies.
It can be said that much more remains unknown about the alliance than is currently known. That is precisely why it has generated so much curiosity among countries outside the grouping.
At the Istanbul meeting, however, officials from the host country made some attempts to satisfy that curiosity, answering some, if not all, of the questions surrounding the alliance.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the alliance was created on the basis of international values such as respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states and non-interference in their internal affairs. However, declaring such values is far easier than adhering to them, as even a cursory look at world politics makes clear.
But there is little doubt that the issue of territorial integrity is of considerable importance to the alliance. Just as alliance member Turkey is fighting separatist Kurdish rebels in the southeast of the country, another member, Pakistan, is confronting increasing activity by independence-seeking armed groups in its Balochistan province.
Hakan Fidan said the Makkah Defense Alliance has no enemies and that its doors are open to other countries. “This alliance is not against any one country, and it is open to all those who share our values in our region,” he said.
Fidan said two things in a single sentence about the possible expansion of the alliance.
First, “open to all”, meaning anyone can join. This statement will give hope to those in Bangladesh who are interested in joining the alliance. Bangladesh has not yet been invited to join, but officials in Dhaka have been expressing their interest for several days.
But Fidan also added the words “in our region.” What exactly does he mean by “region” here?
The founding members of the alliance are primarily countries belonging to the West Asia-Persian Gulf-Mediterranean geopolitical space. Bangladesh, on the other hand, belongs to the South-Southeast Asia-Bay of Bengal region.
Regional media reports discussing potential new members of the alliance have more frequently mentioned Egypt and Syria. There is little doubt that Saudi Arabia is interested in bringing Egypt into the alliance, while Turkey wants to bring Syria under its umbrella.
It is difficult to identify any obvious role for Bangladesh in this Middle East-centred security and political framework.
Various local media reports suggest that there are concerns within the alliance about admitting new members. Any new member could bring additional military and political strength.
But it could also introduce different policy priorities, particularly in foreign affairs, as well as different security perspectives -- all of which could complicate the alliance’s operations.
For example, while Bangladesh could contribute experienced peacekeeping troops to the alliance, Dhaka’s geopolitical and strategic priorities would remain focused on Southeast Asia and the Bay of Bengal.
Bangladesh should aim to maintain cordial relations with all countries in West Asia. Participating in a military alliance in the region would mean becoming involved in local disputes, which would run counter to Bangladesh’s interests.
The debate in Dhaka over the alliance is also examining the India factor from two perspectives.
On the one hand, it is being argued that joining the alliance would strengthen Bangladesh’s security and deter India from aggression.
On the other hand, membership could have precisely the opposite effect.
Joining the alliance would mean establishing formal military ties with Pakistan, which could lead India to view Bangladesh as a threat to its security.
It is difficult to understand how a military alliance can be formed without identifying an “enemy.” No matter how “defensive” an alliance claims to be, why would three countries commit themselves to military action in one another’s defense unless they perceived a threat?
The question becomes even more relevant when one of the three countries possesses around 150 nuclear weapons.
The source of the threat has almost certainly been identified. But the secrecy surrounding it suggests that the alliance’s appeal and effectiveness could be undermined if that country or group were publicly named.
Fidan emphasized certain values in his speech, one of which was “non-interference in anyone’s internal affairs.” This principle was probably raised with Iran in mind.
Since the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979, the Gulf Arab countries have complained that Tehran seeks to export its revolution to Arab states. There is little doubt that Iranian revolutionaries wanted to overthrow the monarchical systems of the Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia.
Iraq invaded Iran in 1980 with financial and other support from Arab countries. Saddam Hussein believed that post-revolutionary Iran could be defeated easily. But after eight years of war, Iraq was forced to accept a ceasefire without achieving its objectives.
The question now is whether the Makkah Defense Alliance was created with Iran in mind. From the perspective of Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries, such an assumption would seem natural.
Although Pakistan maintains friendly relations with Iran, Islamabad has been providing troops for Saudi Arabia’s security for decades.
Turkey’s inclusion sends another message. Recent comments by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggest that war between the two countries may only be a matter of time.
Turkey has been expanding its military presence and political influence in Syria over the past year and a half, developments that Israel views as a threat to its security.
Israel’s plan was to establish dominance across the region after destroying Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and the Assad regime in Syria. The final obstacle was Iran.
But the failure of the US war against Iran has almost derailed Israel’s plan. Israel is now focused on disarming Syria, but Turkey stands in the way.
The announcement of the alliance comes at a time when the security architecture of the Persian Gulf and eastern Mediterranean has almost collapsed.
The joint US-Israeli military operation aimed at overthrowing the Islamic regime in Iran has effectively failed, creating a security vacuum in the region.
Iran has shattered the perception that the US military presence in the Gulf guarantees the security of Saudi Arabia and other Arab monarchies.
There is considerable uncertainty over when, if ever, US military bases in the Gulf will return. It is believed that the Makkah Defense Alliance will attempt to fill this security vacuum.
The initial assessment is that the alliance is primarily focused on Iran and the Houthi group in Yemen. The main threats to Saudi Arabia’s security come from these two sources.
Israel had hoped to become the principal driving force behind a new regional security architecture following Iran’s defeat. Iran disrupted that plan by calling on Arab countries to coordinate their security with Tehran.
The Makkah Defense Alliance has created the possibility of a new geopolitical alignment in West Asia, in which a regional security architecture could emerge outside the orbit of the United States, Israel, and Iran.
Bangladesh’s ruling authorities probably believe that joining the alliance would not only strengthen the country’s economic interests, particularly manpower exports and energy imports, but also enable Dhaka to play a strategic role in this important region.
But are the interests and perspectives of the alliance’s founding members really the same? No. The same would apply to any new members.
The history of the Middle East teaches us that friendships and enmities rarely remain permanent. Loyalties can shift like the sands of the desert. Bangladesh will have to tread very carefully here, lest it stumble into quicksand.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster.

item.title: Chasing blue skies. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the world marks the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, our country is confronted with a sobering truth: Our fight against air pollution is nowhere near where it needs to be.
Bangladesh continues to underestimate the deadly toll of polluted air, even as respiratory illnesses rise, premature deaths increase, and millions of people breathe toxic air every single day.
This day is meant to remind nations that clean air ought to be a fundamental right. For Bangladesh, it should serve as a wake‑up call.
Air pollution has long been one of our most pressing public health emergencies. We consistently rank among the world’s most polluted, with air in our capital and major cities far exceeding safe limits.
Yet, our national response remains fragmented, slow, and often reactive rather than preventive.
From children developing asthma at alarming rates to elderly citizens suffering from chronic diseases to workers needing to work while inhaling air thick with dust, smoke, and chemical emissions, air pollution affects every person but disproportionately affects the marginalized and vulnerable and moves us further away from becoming an equitable nation.
That illegal brick kilns and unregulated factories continue mushrooming is also among our biggest failures, all the while the true number of pollution‑linked deaths remains undercounted, masking the scale of the crisis.
To say we cannot continue down this path would be an understatement. Let today be a reminder that clean air is essential for economic growth, public health, and national stability.
The deadly toll of air pollution is rising, even if official numbers fail to capture its full extent. We must confront this reality with urgency and ambition and recognize that clean air is not a luxury but a necessity if we want to be a healthy, productive, and resilient nation.

item.title: Heeding the call for a liveable environment. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s latest remarks urging collective action for a pollution‑free Bangladesh must be heeded.
Pollution in our country, especially in our major cities, is a daily assault on public health, economic productivity, and the basic livability of our cities. As such, when the head of our government recognizes the issue and calls for unity and urgency, the nation collectively must listen and act.
Of course, our pollution crisis is multidimensional. We have already spoken of our struggling air quality in major cities that routinely falls into hazardous levels in our first editorial, but that is just one aspect of it.
Rivers are choked with industrial waste, sewage, and plastic. Noise pollution has become a constant urban stressor, and unplanned development continues to erode green spaces and natural buffers.
The consequences of this pollution are visible everywhere and affect everyone: rising respiratory illnesses, contaminated water sources, declining biodiversity, and a quality of life that is deteriorating even as the country strives for economic progress.
The prime minister is right to emphasize that this fight cannot be won by the government alone. Pollution is produced by factories that ignore regulations, by corporations that dump waste into canals, by unfit vehicles that belch smoke, and by institutions that treat environmental rules as optional.
A pollution‑free Bangladesh requires responsibility at every level, from policymakers to businesses to ordinary citizens.
A liveable Bangladesh must be the goal, and it is possible only if we treat pollution as the national emergency it is.

item.title: The great digital delusion. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
If you had told a Bangladeshi parent 20 years ago that their child would one day make millions of Taka a month by slapping dye into their hair, dancing wildly on a public overpass, or staging a screaming match with their in-laws in front of a ring light, they would have gently recommended a psychiatric consultation.
Yet, here we are in 2026.
The algorithm is the new deity, the smartphone is the altar, and "views" have somehow become a substitute for value.
Take, for instance, the recent domestic melodrama that dominated our feeds.
The internet exploded with details of infamous TikToker Prince Mamun allegedly joining forces with his second wife to physically assault and evict his own mother and mute sister from their home.
To complete this tragic soap opera, his former partner -- the ever-present "Blue Fairy" Laila -- rushed to the scene to offer shelter to the distressed mother, all under the piercing gaze of rolling smartphones and eager cameras.
Was it genuine heartbreak? Was it an orchestrated PR play? Does anyone even care anymore?
In the hyper-monetized content circus of Bangladesh, human dignity, filial piety, and familial trauma are no longer private matters.
They are mere "hooks" designed to drive retention rates, inflate impressions, and capture ad revenue.
When a society begins to trade its basic moral currency for digital validation, we must pause and ask: Is this truly the "future of work" we were promised?
There was a time when upward social mobility required sweat, late-night study sessions, and decades of professional discipline.
Today, creators like Prince Mamun, Opu Bhai, and Rakib Hossain have bypassed traditional educational paths entirely.
Armed with little more than raw charisma, sensationalism, and an uncanny ability to exploit digital algorithms, these individuals have accumulated fortunes that leave university graduates, engineers, and corporate executives scratching their heads in utter disbelief.
Seeing unlettered influencers pull in tens of thousands of dollars a month while a fresh graduate earns peanuts at an entry-level job has created a profound psychological rift among Bangladeshi youth.
Why endure 16 years of grueling academic pressure only to face a stagnating job market when you can buy a tripod, film a provocative vlog, and land a lucrative brand deal by next Tuesday?
Thousands of young Bangladeshis are abandoning classrooms and technical institutions, harbouring a dangerous ambition: To become "content creators."
They mistake temporary digital notoriety for a legitimate career, unaware that building a life on social media metrics is like building a house on shifting sand.
This entitlement to unearned wealth and status -- where one expects to enjoy all the rewards of social prominence without first putting in the sweat, integrity, or moral dues -- recently manifested in yet another grim headline.
Content creator Ripon Miah, who amassed nearly 1.9 million Facebook followers on the back of quick social media clips, was recently arrested by law enforcement after being accused of abusing his influencer status to harass and ultimately rape a 14-year-old schoolgirl in Netrakona.
Media reports revealed how local influential figures initially attempted to "settle" the heinous crime through an illegal local arbitration ( shalish ), fining him Tk5 lakh and asking him to leave the village while video clips of his apology went viral online.
Ripon’s trajectory -- from a local carpenter to a viral celebrity, and ultimately an accused predator attempting to buy his way out of criminal accountability with easy social media money -- serves as a chilling reminder of what happens when massive influence and financial windfalls precede character, discipline, and hard-earned merit.
It is the ultimate manifestation of wanting to pocket the rewards of success without paying the fundamental dues of human decency, rule of law, and honest labor first.
What these aspiring influencers fail to realize is that content creation is fundamentally unsustainable.
Relevance in the "reel-scrolling" era is ruthlessly ephemeral.
The same audience that elevates an influencer to digital royalty today will swipe away tomorrow without a second thought.
A single change in an algorithm, a shift in audience tastes, or a temporary suspension of monetization can instantly reduce a "social media millionaire" to complete financial oblivion.
Worse still, this desperate race for virality has given birth to a sinister, predatory ecosystem.
The promise of social media fame is no longer just a distraction -- it has turned into a dangerous trap.
Media reports across Bangladesh have documented tragic instances where young girls from vulnerable backgrounds were lured with promises of becoming "TikTok stars" or landed roles in viral videos.
Instead, they faced horrific fates -- abduction, sexual assault, and human trafficking networks operating under the guise of talent agencies and creator houses.
The tragic reality is that while a select few pocket cash from ad networks, scores of impressionable youths pay for this illusion with their lives, freedom, and dignity.
Even for those who manage to stay on the legitimate side of the law, the golden goose of online monetization is growing tired.
Platform giants like YouTube continuously refine their Partner Program policies.
In their ongoing efforts to appease advertisers, platforms are cracking down on repetitive content, sensationalized clickbait, low-effort clips, and ethical violations.
For Bangladeshi creators reliant on sensationalism or repurposed content, the revenue gravy train is slowing down.
While YouTube periodically adjusts regional monetization pathways, making it technically easier for localized content to earn revenue, the bar for qualifying content is rising sharply.
Algorithms are increasingly penalizing vulgarity, family drama, and synthetic outrage.
When the platforms decide to clean up their digital storefronts, hundreds of creators who traded their education for short-term views will find themselves with neither a steady paycheck nor transferable skills for the real world.
This brings us to an inescapable truth: Mobile-generated content can never ethically or practically replace real labour, technical expertise, and formal education.
A nation cannot run on reaction videos, pranks, and unboxing clips.
Who will design the bridges, manage the power grids, or write the software systems that keep our economy moving forward?
Who will treat the sick, harvest the crops, teach the next generation, or manufacture the very goods that influencers unbox on camera?
True labor builds tangible value. It instills discipline, produces tangible progress, and offers a level of personal self-respect that no amount of digital "likes" can ever match.
Formal and technical education are not merely decorative certificates but are the structural framework of a functional society.
They impart problem-solving capabilities, critical thinking, and resilient skills that withstand algorithmic shifts, economic downturns, and platform updates.
There is no shame in leveraging modern technology to express oneself, share stories, or build an audience.
But when content creation degrades into public spectacles of familial abuse -- where a mother's tears are treated as engagement fuel -- it ceases to be entertainment.
It becomes a sign of moral degradation masquerading as entrepreneurship.
We must strip away the illusion surrounding "influencer culture."
Let the youth enjoy their short-form videos, but let them also understand the clear line between a temporary hobby and a lifelong profession.
Real success is not measured in subscriber counts, brand deals, or viral scandals.
It is measured in the quiet dignity of honest work, the pursuit of real knowledge, and the enduring strength of human integrity.
In the end, when the screens go black and the servers shut down, it is honest, physical, and intellectual labor that will keep the world turning -- long after the last reel has been swiped away.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

Things that lose money should close down. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Tea is an important part of life. I am an Englishman, and I would be betraying my entire culture if I didn't agree with that. But to say that being able to consume tea is important is not the same statement as trying to insist that certain tea plantations are important.
After all, as Adam Smith himself pointed out, “the sole purpose of all production is consumption.” As long as there is tea that we can brew up, the survival of a specific tea producer is of no matter.
Even the survival of an entire sector of tea production in one country doesn't matter. It's the being able to consume that matters, nor where produced nor who by.
This is the correct starting point for a consideration of this : “A revolving fund at a 6% interest rate to tackle the financing crisis in the tea sector.”
The inflation rate, at 8%, is higher than this 6%. The base rate at the central bank is near one and a half times that 6% at 9.5%. Commercial bank loans are at 12% and up.
So, the insistence here is that tea plantations should, effectively, be gifted free money.
Yes, obviously, the hope is that they'll pay it back, the money itself. But if they've not got to pay for the use of the money -- pay a real interest rate -- then that is the same statement as they get to use the money for free.
That's not a good idea.
The useful description of economics is that it's the study of the allocation of scarce resources. Resources are things like land, labor, and capital. We need to allocate them as best we can so as to make ourselves, collectively, as rich as we can. This means allocating those resources efficiently.
For there are always alternative uses of those resources. We could use the land of tea plantations for tea. We could put goats on it or solar panels. We could just go and stare at the awesome majesty of the mountains.
Whichever of those uses produces the greatest value to us consumers is the most efficient use of those mountain slopes.
We are gaining the greatest increase in the enjoyment of our lives by the use of those mountains to produce the greater value we can enjoy.
This is also obviously true of labor, of capital, and so on. We want to use our limited supplies of everything to produce the greatest amount that we can consume.
So, if the tea plantations cannot even pay us for the use of our money -- an interest rate below the inflation rate really is free money to a business, a loss to the rest of us -- then at least some of those tea plantations should no longer be in business.
They are not adding value, they are consuming more resources than they produce in value. They are a net loss to our society.
This is true of anything and everything in our society. Those things that are, nominally, businesses must produce more value than it costs to run them.
Otherwise they are all making us poorer -- the resources they consume are greater than the value of production, and yes, this really does mean they are making us all, in aggregate, poorer.
For we could devote those resources to things which add value, not subtract it.
If tea plantations can only survive by getting free money from the rest of us, then tea plantations should go bankrupt instead. Or at least some of them should, which will reduce the amount of tea produced. We'll all have to pay more for our tea, and that's the way the surviving ones will profit.
This is, of course, true of every other form of production in our economy. If it requires subsidy, then that's the grand clue that that form of production should not exist. Or, at least, less of it should.
I agree that it's a fairly harsh point to make, but things that lose money really should close down.
It's also fairly harsh to use tea plantations as the example, but, as at the top, I'm an Englishman. Tea is important; we really should get this right.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Losing our progress to extreme heat. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We are shocked to learn that, as per a study by the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) and the Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP), informal workers collectively lose an estimated Tk50,630 crore in wages annually because of extreme heat.
This is a staggering economic blow that is equivalent to 0.91% of GDP. To dismiss it as a distant climate threat would be a grave error—it is a present economic crisis.
With outdoor workers missing up to 24 days of work each year due to unbearable temperatures, while indoor workers are also losing about 14 days too, we must remember that these are people who already earn below a living wage, and every lost day pushes them deeper into financial insecurity.
While we cannot control the weather, we can reiterate that such extreme heat is as a result of climate change, and this global warming has been caused by the developed world.
That they continue to not do their part in supporting developing nations such as ours suffering disproportionately from this crisis is among the greatest global failures of our time.
With that said, Bangladesh too must implement heat‑response measures immediately, from investing in cooling centers to better heat‑resilient housing upgrades for informal settlements.
There is also the need for a more humanitarian approach to the work itself, with mandatory rest breaks and shade for outdoor workers and the necessary medical support for workers exposed to chronic heat.
Aspirations of becoming an equitable nation will never be realized if we fail to recognize that the majority of our working population continue to suffer and are unable to work to their full potential.

item.title: Reviving jute means supporting farmers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For years now, we have been speaking of the potential of jute, and for the need to support its production.
To that end, that farmers are struggling to receive fair prices for jute after a year of promising yield is disappointing.
Jute is not just another crop. It is a national asset, a symbol of rural livelihoods, and a sector with enormous potential for value-added exports.
Yet, the farmers who sustain this “golden fiber" continue to face a market that does not value their work.
High production costs, exploitative middlemen, and inconsistent government procurement have created a situation where farmers bear all the risks but receive none of the rewards.
The contradiction is glaring. Bangladesh speaks proudly of diversifying exports, expanding jute‑based industries, and promoting eco‑friendly alternatives to plastic.
Yet, these ambitions ring hollow when farmers in major producing districts cannot earn enough to survive.
It goes without saying that a sector cannot thrive when its foundation is collapsing, and the authorities concerned should treat this moment with urgency.
Farmers need fair and predictable prices, not seasonal fluctuations that leave them vulnerable, and need protection from syndicates that manipulate the market. Supporting this industry also means ensuring farmers have access to storage and transport so they are not forced to sell at distress rates.
Above all, they need a policy framework that recognizes jute for its present and future importance and supports it accordingly.
If Bangladesh wants jute to remain a pillar of its rural economy and export future, it must ensure that the people who grow it are not left behind.

item.title: Two statutes older than the internet are setting startup policy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Somewhere in Dhaka right now, a software company with paying customers in 40 countries is being incorporated in Wyoming. The founder is Bangladeshi, the engineers are Bangladeshi, and the salaries will be paid in taka. The company will be American, and making it so costs about $500.
The reason is Stripe. It does not support Bangladesh, and neither does PayPal in any form that lets a business here receive and withdraw revenue. Sell software to the world, and you need a payments provider, and every serious one requires an entity incorporated in a country on its list.
A private company's compliance list has become the most influential piece of corporate policy affecting Bangladeshi start-ups. That should trouble us more than the funding chart does.
We treat incorporation as a tax question. It is a question of what a company may sign.
A Bangladeshi private limited company cannot hold a Stripe account. It cannot issue a SAFE or a convertible note, neither of which has statutory recognition under the Companies Act 1994.
It cannot give a fund a liquidation preference backed by a forum that resolves in months. It cannot be acquired by a foreign buyer without prior Bangladesh Bank approval on transfer of control.
Each of those is a contract, and a Delaware or Singapore entity signs all of them on a Tuesday. Founders know the offshore parent will be required eventually and that doing it later is expensive, so they do it first.
The tax explanation has run out.
The Finance Act 2026 rebuilt the startup regime. A registered startup under Tk 100 crore in turnover gets a nine-year growth period, a turnover tax cut to zero across it, a loss carry-forward that survives changes in shareholding, and VAT exemption until June 2035.
For a loss-making early-stage company, the tax position in Dhaka is now at least as good as Singapore's. FEID Circular 1 of March 2026 then lets banks clear repatriation of share proceeds up to Tk 100 crore without central bank sign-off, 10 times the old ceiling, in five days.
These are serious reforms, and the people behind them deserve credit. But founders kept incorporating abroad through both.
One condition runs through the package. A startup, for these purposes, is a company incorporated under the Companies Act 1994. The relief reaches only the founders who stayed and answers a question they were not asking.
Two groups leave for unrelated reasons. Venture-track companies flip at the first institutional round, because a fund requires an offshore parent before it wires.
Bootstrapped software companies flip in week one, because a payments provider requires a listed-country entity before it processes.
The second group is larger by headcount and invisible by construction.
When we read that start-ups raised six million dollars in the first half of 2026 and conclude the ecosystem is finished, we are reading a register of who chose Bangladeshi paperwork.
Foreign exchange is governed by an Act from 1947, written before the country existed. Companies are governed by an Act from 1994, written before the commercial internet.
Circulars have patched around both for two years, and a circular cannot create an instrument the underlying Act does not contemplate.
The July 2025 Share Swap circular lets shareholders swap operating company shares for offshore holdco shares with no capital leaving Bangladesh: Useful, and a bridge built toward the offshore parent rather than a removal of the reason to want one.
A startup schedule inside the Companies Act would do most of the work. Statutory recognition for convertible instruments. Primacy for shareholder agreements over articles, so preferences and drag-along bind as written.
A commercial forum with a fixed clock, because investors are pricing years and months, would change that price. And publication of Bangladeshi-founded funding beside Bangladesh-domiciled funding, because a country cannot tax what its statistics decline to see.
I have raised money into a Bangladeshi cap table and into a Singapore one. The difference was never conviction about where to build. It was that one legal vocabulary had a word for the instrument the investor held.
Six million dollars is a number about paperwork. The companies are here.
Hussain M Elius co-founded Pathao and founded Wind. He is the author of "Moving Bangladesh: The Origin Story of Pathao."

item.title: The economic impact of diabetes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Diabetes is a chronic condition that occurs when the body cannot produce enough or effectively use insulin. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that allows glucose from food to enter the body’s cells, where it is converted into energy needed by muscles and tissues to function.
As a result, a person with diabetes does not absorb glucose properly, and glucose stays circulating in the blood (hyperglycemia), damaging tissues over time. This damage leads to life-threatening health complications.
According to the Diabetes Atlas published by the International Diabetic Federation, as of 2024, 589 million adults (20-79 years) are living with diabetes worldwide.
Diabetes imposes a large economic burden on any national healthcare system; estimated figures show healthcare expenditures on diabetes accounted for 11.8% of the total healthcare expenditure in the world in 2025.
About 95% of the countries spend 5% or more of their total healthcare dollars on diabetes. Global health expenditures to prevent and treat diabetes and its complications surpassed $376 billion in 2010, and by 2030, this number will be close to $500bn.
Research results show that there remains a large disparity in healthcare spending on diabetes between regions and countries. More than 80% of the global expenditures on diabetes are made in the world's most economically rich countries, not in the low- and middle-income countries where 80% of people with diabetes live.
Recent studies drew three major conclusions on the overall economic impact of diabetes
First , diabetes imposes a large financial burden on people with diabetes and their families. The size of this burden depends on their economic status and the social insurance policies of the countries in which they live.
Individuals with diabetes and their families in developing countries pay a larger share of the expenditure because of the poorer organized systems of medical care insurance and/or lack of governmental provision of medical services.
In the poorest countries, people with diabetes and their families bear almost the whole cost of whatever medical care they can afford.
Second , at the societal level, diabetes leads to loss in productivity and economic growth. It is estimated that the US economy lost over $100bn as a result of lost earnings due to lost workdays, restricted activity days, lower productivity at work, mortality, and permanent disability caused by diabetes.
Such losses are even larger in poorer countries relative to GDP because premature death due to diabetes occurs at much younger ages.
Finally , the largest economic burden caused by diabetes is the monetary value associated with disability and loss of life as a result of the disease itself and its related complications, including heart, kidney, eye, and foot disease.
Economists have used different methods to value disability and loss of life associated with diseases, and the most appropriate method is still debated. Yet, no matter what method is used, it is very likely the economic burden that is measured by the monetary value associated with this disability and loss of life would be far larger than the estimated economic burden using measures described above.
Most people with diabetes live in less developed regions of the world. Even in the region with the lowest prevalence (Africa), according to the IDF Diabetes Atlas (9th Edition) released for 2019, diabetes was responsible for an estimated 366,200 deaths in the IDF Africa Region.
Diabetes has reached epidemic proportions worldwide. Every year, more people are diagnosed with diabetes, yet there are still many (more than 50%) people who have diabetes and do not know it. A small survey in Bangladesh indicated that the prevalence of diabetes in Bangladesh in populations aged over 15 years is between 2% and 5%. This type of similarity is also found in most of the underdeveloped countries.
Since diabetes is a life-long and non-episodic disease that affects many other organs of the body, a comprehensive and good pathological support-based treatment is needed to manage it.
Dr Muhammad Abdul Mazid is formerly secretary and chairman, NBR, and National Council Member of the Diabetic Association of Bangladesh.

Bangladesh hospital wards crowded as measles toll nears grim 1,000-child mark. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades is nearing the grim milestone of 1,000 child deaths, as a devastating epidemic sweeps through the country and crowded hospital wards fill with struggling babies.

Cries of sick children and the hiss of oxygen machines fill the air at Dhaka’s Shishu Hospital, where Rima Akter keeps a vigil beside her nine-month-old son.

“Just an hour ago, a child died, and they wheeled him out in front of us,” 30-year-old Akter told AFP on Thursday.

“We saw two children die today.”

Akter’s son Sabit Haque is one of scores filling the children’s hospital’s measles wards.

At least 986 children have died since March, while suspected and confirmed cases have surged past 180,000, according to the latest health ministry figures.

Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught.

Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems.

Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable.

The South Asian nation of 170 million has rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but case numbers continue to climb.

More than 1,000 suspected cases are reported daily.

‘Very weak’

“I’ve been running to and from multiple hospitals since July to get my son the proper treatment,” said Sanjana Islam Modina, 19, cradling her six-month-old son Ayan, who has an oxygen tube fixed to his nose.

Small dark spots covered Ayan’s head, fading from the angry red rash left by measles.

He was first admitted to hospital with pneumonia in July, then contracted measles before finally securing a bed at the capital’s specialised children’s hospital in mid-August.

Ayan spent 15 days in intensive care, before improving enough to return to the dedicated measles ward.

The hospital currently has 101 children admitted with suspected or confirmed measles.

“His lungs were already very weak from the pneumonia, then with measles his breathing was affected more,” Modina told AFP, while trying to soothe her wailing baby.

“He’s been on oxygen constantly for the last five days.”

Most cases recorded in Bangladesh during the current outbreak have been among children aged between six months and five years.

Doctors say many of the children arriving at hospital are already critically ill, with malnutrition further weakening their ability to fight the virus.

Ayan has also been diagnosed as malnourished.

“The doctors gave my son a special milk specifically designed for malnourished children,” said Modina, wiping sweat from his tiny forehead.

‘Devastating’

The outbreak has exposed gaps in Bangladesh’s efforts to protect its youngest.

SM Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for health, called the outbreak “devastating”.

Bangladesh had previously made major advances in vaccination against infectious diseases, but a measles drive planned for 2024 was delayed by the uprising that toppled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

Workers’ strikes and political instability delayed a 2025 campaign.

The country has since rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but the number of cases continues to climb.

“There was a gap of a significant number of children missing the doses,” Hyder said.

“Healthcare workers… are vaccinating these children to close the gap.”

Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), said Bangladesh should consider a broader vaccination campaign to contain the outbreak.

Rahman said public awareness was also crucial, stressing preventive measures including isolating infected children, handwashing and the use of masks by caregivers.

Worried mother Akter needs no reminder of how quickly the sickness can spread.

“We are aware of how contagious this disease is; our son was first admitted for bronchitis,” she said.

“After being released, we had to come back for measles.”

Header image: Children receive treatment for measles, at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital & Institute in Dhaka on Sept 3, 2026. — AFP

The scale of Bangladesh’s tannery waste problem is troubling, but there is certainly an economic opportunity hidden within it that we would be remiss to overlook.
Experts estimate that properly processing tannery waste and turning it into value-added products could generate an additional Tk2,000-3,000 crore in annual revenue.
This is precisely the kind of opportunity Bangladesh should be pursuing: One that can simultaneously address an environmental crisis, create new industries, generate employment, and also strengthen an important export sector.
For years, tannery waste has largely been treated as something to be disposed of rather than a resource to be recovered, and the consequences have been severe: Poorly managed waste has contributed to pollution around the Savar Tannery Industrial Estate, adding further pressure to already struggling waterways.
At a time when our rivers are being overwhelmed by industrial and other forms of waste, continuing with such a linear approach is simply unsustainable.
Yet, the materials currently being discarded have considerable potential.
Collagen-rich waste can be converted into products such as gelatin, industrial tallow, bio-fertilizer, and leather board, while chrome shavings and other by-products can have applications ranging from capsule shells to other industrial materials.
Even treatment-plant sludge has reportedly been used to produce tiles and bricks.
What is needed now is a serious transition towards a circular economy -- which will require investment in waste-processing facilities, green financing, appropriate incentives, research and development, and stronger links between waste processors and markets.
The government must also address the industry's environmental compliance problems. Environmental protection and economic growth should not be presented as opposing objectives; in this case, they can reinforce one another.
The opportunity before us is clear: Instead of allowing tannery waste to become another burden on our rivers and communities, Bangladesh should turn it into a valuable resource. Doing so would be good environmental policy -- and smart economics.

Feeding our future. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We agree with the State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj that providing midday meals to schoolchildren must be viewed as a right rather than an act of charity.
His remarks come at an important time, as Bangladesh seeks to improve both access to and the quality of primary education.
A child cannot be expected to concentrate on lessons while hungry, and for many children from low-income households, the meal received at school may be the most integral part of their daily nutrition.
A properly designed and implemented school feeding program can, therefore, do much more than put food on a plate: It can improve attendance, concentration, learning outcomes, and ultimately a child's prospects in life.
This is particularly important if the government's stated ambition is to ensure that no child remains out of school, and that every child receives a proper education.
Investment in classrooms and textbooks will only go so far if children arrive at school hungry or leave because their families cannot afford to meet their basic needs.
However, recognizing this as a right also means recognizing the government's responsibility to deliver it properly. There can be no room for substandard food, irregular supplies, wastage, or corruption.
Thus, the minister's warning that poor-quality or unsuitable food will not be accepted is welcome.
Transparency and accountability must be built into every stage of the program, from procurement and transportation to distribution at individual schools. Teachers, parents and local communities should have meaningful avenues to monitor what children are receiving, and report irregularities.
Most importantly, the program must be expanded carefully and sustainably so that children across the country, regardless of where they live or their family's financial circumstances, can benefit.
A midday meal should never be something a child has to feel grateful for. It is an investment in their health, education and future -- and, by extension, in Bangladesh's future.
